utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-87-T, the Prosecutor versus Milutinovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. We're delighted to see that all parties are present and ready to proceed. Mr. O'Sullivan, we understand that you intend to open the Defence case with an opening speech for Mr. Milutinovic in terms of Rule 84. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and good morning honourable Trial Chamber and good morning to my friends from the Office of the Prosecutor. Your Honour, three months ago the Prosecution made oral submissions pursuant to Rule 98 bis at the conclusion of its case in chief. The Prosecution made its submissions, we say, based on its selection and interpretation of some of the evidence in this case. Before Mr. Milutinovic calls his first witness, we ask the Trial Chamber to bear in mind the following matters while hearing the evidence which Mr. Milutinovic will call in his Defence. The essence of the Prosecution's position is that Mr. Milutinovic furthered the alleged joint criminal enterprise by exercising some of his powers, as understood and interpreted by the Prosecution, as the president of Serbia, and that he omitted to fulfil his obligations as the president of Serbia; in other words, commission by omission. Let us be clear straight away. It is Mr. Milutinovic's position that there was no joint criminal enterprise, as alleged in the indictment or otherwise. Furthermore, his position is that the evidence adduced so far in this case and the evidence he will lead during his defence case will demonstrate that Mr. Milutinovic was never involved in any criminal conduct, either individually or in concert with others or within any sort of conspiracy. He dutifully fulfilled his obligations as president of Serbia and he did nothing illegal, either by commission or omission. The authority and competence of the president of Serbia did not include any of the powers alleged by the Prosecution, and the evidence in this case will show the Prosecution is incorrect. Mr. Milutinovic never, in fact, exercised the powers alleged by the Prosecution. His acts and conducts in relation to Kosovo and Metohija are those of a politician who was working and using his best efforts to find a peaceful, true political solution to the problems which existed and to avoid any harm to all citizens of Serbia. In short we say that Mr. Milutinovic, and the evidence will show this, never misused any of his authority as president of Serbia and he never derogated from his responsibilities or refused to act in a positive and constructive manner as president of Serbia. Now, a moment ago we made reference to the Prosecution's position that Mr. Milutinovic furthered the alleged joint criminal enterprise by omitting to exercise competencies conferred on him by the constitution of Serbia. And during its 98 bis submissions, the Prosecution stated that it considers the source of the duty of the president to act is his oath of office and his responsibility to the citizens of the Republic of Serbia. The Prosecution relied on two provisions of the constitution of Serbia, which I will quote for short. Article 86 is the oath of office and it states: "I swear that I shall devote all my forces to the preservation of sovereignty and integrity of the territory of the Republic of Serbia, to the realisation of human and civil freedoms and rights, to the observance and defence of the constitution and laws; to the preserving of peace and welfare of all the citizens of the Republic of Serbia, and that I shall conscientiously and responsibly meet all my duties." The second provision is Article 88 which is one sentence, it reads: "The President of the Republic shall be responsible to the citizens of the Republic of Serbia." But the Prosecution explicitly stated that it relies on these two provisions of the constitution of Serbia in its claim that Mr. Milutinovic had a duty to act to make it more difficult for the other members of the alleged joint criminal enterprise to implement the objective of the joint criminal enterprise. Mr. Milutinovic disputes this incomplete and unfounded reading of the constitution, and he disagrees with the Prosecution's assessment of the evidence in this case so far. For this reason, to address the constitutional issues, Mr. Milutinovic's first witness will be Professor Ratko Markovic, who will provide expert testimony on the constitution. Professor Markovic will provide the Trial Chamber with the proper context, reading, and interpretation of the -- I was saying that Professor Markovic will provide the Trial Chamber with the proper context, reading, and interpretation of the constitution of the Republic of Serbia and the constitution of the FRY and the legislation concerning the authority and competence of the president of Serbia. This evidence will show that the authority and competence vested in the president of Serbia is limited and restrictive. His authority and competence is restricted in particular concerning the relationship between the president and the Government of Serbia and the president and the National Assembly of Serbia as well as other institutions and agencies within the republic. The president has no means to commit any of the offences alleged by the Prosecution, either by acts or omission. In addition, the expert evidence of Professor Markovic will show that as a member of the Supreme Defence Council, the president of Serbia exercises no command, control, or authority over the VJ, the MUP, or "Serb Forces," as the Prosecution uses the term "Serb Forces" in the indictment. Only the federal president, the president of FRY, has the legal powers and mechanisms to exercise command and control. The president of Serbia, like the president of Montenegro, is a member of the Supreme Defence Council. The Supreme Defence Council, as Professor Markovic will explain, is an advisory body provided for in the constitution of the FRY. Professor Markovic will also give evidence which will show that the amendments to the constitution -- or the constitutional amendments of 1989, 1990, and 1992 were not discriminatory against Kosovar Albanians. His testimony in this regard will provide the proper legal, historical, and social context for the changes which occurred in the legal system in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Your Honour, the Prosecution alleges that Mr. Milutinovic's responsibility under the constitution is his failure to raise an alarm in the corridors of government. The evidence in this case and the evidence we will lead will show that the corridors of government were ringing with the problems of Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 and 1999. The armed insurrection of the KLA and their terrorist activities and the measures and the concrete steps taken to improve the situation in Kosovo and Metohija attempts to find a lasting political solution to keep Kosovo and Metohija within Serbia as an autonomous province with full respect for all groups and minorities living there. And might I add at this point that the problems and challenges were as great then as they are today as we can see from the fact that the process for finding a solution for Kosovo and Metohija is still ongoing in the UN and within the Contact Group. During the Defence case the Trial Chamber will hear about the policy of the government of national assembly towards Kosovo and Metohija, you will hear about efforts that were undertaken to improve the situation within the province on education, humanitarian relief, providing safe and secure living conditions. The Trial Chamber will hear evidence about the attempts throughout 1998 and the early part of 1999 to achieve a comprehensive agreement on substantial self-governance in Kosovo and Metohija from the men who were directly involved in the process. Furthermore, you will hear the role Mr. Milutinovic played in this process, the efforts he expended to achieve a successful solution to the problem, and his attitudes towards the process itself. Mr. Milutinovic asks how, based on the evidence, it can seriously be contended that he failed to fulfil his obligations under the constitution and laws of his country and under international humanitarian law. His acts and conduct are those of a person who intended to avoid having harm done to others. His acts are those of a responsible and individual politician, who did all he could to find a viable, peaceful solution for Kosovo for the benefit of all its citizens. From the evidence at this point we know this about Mr. Milutinovic's activities and state of mind. I'll remind you that following the decision by the Government of Serbia on the 11th of March, 1998, to establish a delegation to negotiate with the Albanian leadership in Kosovo and Metohija, delegation headed by Professor Markovic, Mr. Milutinovic made a statement on the 18th of March, 1998, and he said this, and I quote: "Procrastination and delay to start in direct political dialogue is ... unjustified and damaging. "In my capacity as president of the republic, I am prepared to be the guarantor of such discussions based on the principles of preserving territorial integrity and of including in the agenda the issue of self-government for Kosovo and Metohija within Serbia." Mr. Milutinovic in this statement calls for a solution "by political means, peaceful methods, and dialogue." He calls on the three plus three group to proceed immediately to the implementation on the agreement of the normalisation of education. And he states this: "I point out that my conviction that the future of the citizens of Kosovo and Metohija as well as those in Serbia and in all our country does not lie in ethnic, religious, or cultural closing-up and divisions, but in peace, equality, integration, and life together." The Chamber will recall that on the 31st of March, 1998, UN Security Council Resolution 1160 expressly makes reference to Mr. Milutinovic's statement of the 18th of March, and the UN Security Council calls on the parties to do exactly what Mr. Milutinovic had advocated. You will see and hear that the evidence in this case is that throughout 1998 Mr. Milutinovic made similar sincere and convincing speeches to support and encourage the process of dialogue and agreement, urging all citizens of Serbia, including those living in Kosovo and Metohija, to live together in peace. He personally invited Albanian political leaders to meet with the Markovic delegation. He accompanied the Markovic delegation to Pristina on several occasions. He directly supported the implementation of the education agreement. He met and worked with Ambassador Hill to support attempts at international mediation of the Kosovo problem. He met with minority leaders from Kosovo and Metohija, in support of an agreement on self-governance. He denounced extremism and violence as a means to a political end. The Chamber has also seen UN Security Council Resolution 1199 of the 23rd of September, 1998, and to be mindful of the observations made by Mr. Milutinovic at a session of the Supreme Defence Council held on the 4th of October, 1998, where in relation to this resolution and the threat of NATO strikes, Mr. Milutinovic stated, I quote: "... When you take a close look at the whole UN resolution, item after item, we have practically fulfilled everything. If there is something else we have to do, then we should not let this strike happen." Your Honour, of particular importance and significance we say are the events in November 1998 that you'll hear about where Mr. Milutinovic travelled to Pristina twice within a matter of days and met with leaders of minority political parties in Belgrade, including Albanians. These are the events surrounding the joint proposal on the agreement on the political framework on self-governance in Kosovo and Metohija. Evidence presented during the Defence case will give the Trial Chamber first-hand accounts of the events regarding the elaboration of this agreement and which led to a statement made by Mr. Milutinovic in Pristina on the 18th of November, 1998. Can I remind you of some of the things he said in that statement. Mr. Milutinovic said: Serbia is firmly committed to having the problems in Kosovo and Metohija resolved politically. Serbia is a civil state, and it does not divide its citizens according to their national, religious, or any other background. But at the same time, Serbia is a multi-ethnic, multi-confessional, and multi-cultural state, guaranteeing to all national communities additional rights for the preservation and expression of their national identity, script, language, religion, customs, culture, and tradition. Mr. Milutinovic stated: I would like to underline that peace and common life are possible in Kosmet only with genuine, not just formal equality of all national communities. This has been confirmed by the fact that we have honoured all obligations and deadlines set forth in the agreements with the international community, that civilian structures are functioning and getting stronger by the day in Kosmet, that the situation in all fields, particularly economic, social, and humanitarian is being increasingly normalised in Kosmet. He stated: As far as political framework is concerned, legal, i.e., constitutional framework in our country is broad enough to ensure consistent implementation of international standards in the field of protection of rights of national communities with full respect of the existing practice. Once the above is honoured, he said, the form is clear, democratic self-governance in the Republic of Serbia and consequently in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In that respect, it should be clear to all that any solution for Kosmet has to respect the territorial integrity and sovereignty and internationally recognised borders of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in accordance with the fundamental principles of the Charter of the United Nations, Helsinki Final Act and the OSCE Paris charter. And he concluded these statements by broadening the importance of a resolution bonding it to the greater region. He said: With all those measures we wish to encourage trust and accelerate the political process. Only in this can we see the preconditions to solve the problems in Kosovo and Metohija which will enable the national communities to realise democratic self-governance, guarantee territorial integrity and sovereignty of our state, ensure peace and development in Kosovo and Metohija, but also stability in the region of the Balkans and south-eastern Europe, and inclusion of the peoples and the States from these parts in broader political, economic, cultural, and other integration processes, organisations, and institutions. Your Honour, we've been saying that during our Defence case the Trial Chamber will hear important testimony about the attempts to improve the situation in Kosovo and Metohija and to conclude a comprehensive agreement on self-governance. We also ask the Trial Chamber to bear in mind the significance of this process in 1998 and 1999 in the light of the evidence given by General Klaus Naumann, who testified that NATO did not and could not engage with the KLA because certain NATO countries had denounced the KLA as terrorists in 1998. Now, we know it is not uncommon for states to refuse to recognise, let alone negotiate, with groups or organisations which are considered to be terrorist. We have seen this played out in today's world when groups or organisations hit office towers in New York city, when train stations are bombed in Madrid or London or most recently when individuals took over a mosque in Islamabad. My point is this: The government institutions in the FRY and Serbia did not refuse to engage in dialogue with the Albanian leadership in Kosovo and Metohija, including the leadership of the KLA. On the contrary, governments and legislatures at both levels, the federal and republic levels, took concrete steps in 1998 and 1999 to improve the situation and work for a peaceful solution in Kosovo. The Chamber knows already that these efforts began in earnest in the spring of 1998. That's when the delegation headed by Professor Markovic was formed to engage the Albanian leadership in dialogue. Special Envoys were appointed to bolster that process. Agreement on the implementation of the education agreement was achieved. Humanitarian relief programmes were established. Agreements were reached with President Yeltsin of the Russian Federation, Ambassador Holbrooke and the OSCE in June and October respectively to ensure an international presence on the territory of Serbia while a political solution was sought. Invitation after invitation was sent to the Albanian political representatives by the Serbian. Only once did the Albanian representatives sit down with the state delegation. These invitations included letters sent to the leadership of the KLA, and here we're thinking of Mr. Demaqi. At Rambouillet and Paris a state delegation was sent by the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia attended meetings and requested on numerous occasions to meet face-to-face with the Albanian delegation whose ranks included leading members of the KLA including its president Mr. Hashim Thaqi. Some might say, perhaps of quite understandable reasons that groups or organisations that resort to violence to effect political change should not be recognised as legitimate interlocutors. This certainly cannot be said for the events of 1998 and 1999 in this case. The contribution made by Mr. Milutinovic in seeking a peaceful solution in Kosovo and Metohija was significant. In addition to the examples I've mentioned you will hear evidence about Mr. Milutinovic attending a meeting of the Government of Serbia in October 1998 shortly after the Holbrooke-Milosevic Agreement, where Mr. Milutinovic informed the government about the details of that agreement. Then Mr. Milutinovic travelled to Pristina in September and November 1998, he met briefly with local officials to provide information on the political, economic, and security situation in Kosovo and Metohija. The Prosecution also alleges that the FRY/Serb delegation and Mr. Milutinovic in particular intentionally obstructed the Rambouillet/Paris meetings held in February and March 1999. And the Prosecution contends that the intention was to create a window of opportunity, provoking a war with NATO, in order to carry out the JCE. Putting aside the facts for a moment, we say that this position is untenable and defies common sense. But when we turn to the facts, the evidence in this case, we now know that to lay the blame at the feet of the Serbs for the failure at Rambouillet and Paris was misleading and cynical. We know from the evidence in this case that the Serb/FRY delegation were in general agreement with the political components of the Rambouillet agreement. We know that the Serb side, including Mr. Milutinovic, had been working for the better part of 1998 on such an agreement which was put in final form, as you know, in Pristina in November 1998. We know that the Albanian side was not prepared to accept the political component of the Rambouillet Agreement as it was written into that agreement. We know that at the 11th hour there was a non-disclosed side deal between the US secretary of state and the Albanians. It was openly admitted by Mr. Surroi, a witness here, who was a member of that delegation, and reluctantly acknowledged by Ambassador Petritsch, one of the Contact Group negotiators, who added the caveat that what individual states do at international conferences cannot be attributed to the Contact Group. We say it is absolutely disingenuous to suggest that a side letter between the US Secretary of State and the Albanian delegation on a referendum in Kosovo and Metohija on independence is in some way an innocuous by-product of international relations and meetings. And this side letter went to the heart of the matter: The territorial integrity and sovereignty of the FRY and Serbia. Your Honour, there was no reluctance on the part of the state delegation to engage in serious and meaningful discussion at Rambouillet and Paris, and you'll hear that during our Defence. Indeed they requested on numerous occasions face-to-face meetings with the Albanians, to have the Contact Group principle signed by both delegations, and to be given the entire agreement for review at the beginning of the conference. I would add that even after the Albanian delegation refused to sign the Contact Group non-negotiable principles, the FRY/Serb delegation signed them unilaterally and presented them to the Contact Group. But during the Defence case you will hear that Mr. Milutinovic arrived at Rambouillet at the end of the first week of the meetings. The meetings at that point were scheduled to end after one week. You will hear he came to assist and to encourage a resolution to the situation and that he remained to work towards the success of those meetings. You will hear that the talks in Paris in March 1999, the Serb/FRY delegation was prepared to finalise the political elements of the agreement and to discuss the scope and character of an international presence in Kosovo and Metohija, just as they had indicated to the Contact Group when talks ended in Rambouillet in February. You will hear that Mr. Milutinovic supported this position, both within the context of the Paris meetings and publicly in statements made outside those meetings. The Chamber will hear that in Paris Mr. Milutinovic stated that: The state delegation has submitted proposals to the Contact Group concerning political elements of the agreement ... without changing its essence and that they were prepared to sign. He also stated that when the political component was finalised they would be willing to discuss the scope and character of implementation. You will hear evidence that Mr. Milutinovic's position and message was consistently that if the agreement on autonomy and self-government for Kosovo and Metohija is stable and good then the deployment of foreign troops on the territory of Serbia would not be necessary. Only a bad solution would necessitate the intervention of foreign soldiers to enforce it. You will hear that Mr. Milutinovic brought to bear his long experience as a diplomat and as the foreign minister -- the former foreign minister of the FRY during Rambouillet and Paris. When listening to this evidence we ask you to consider the following facts in this case. Mr. Milutinovic had served as an ambassador in the SFRY Ministry of Foreign Affairs as head of state for press, information, and culture from 1987 to 1989. He was the SFRY and FRY ambassador to Greece from 1989 to 1995. He was the FRY foreign minister from 1995 to 1997. You will hear that Mr. Milutinovic knew all the Contact Group foreign ministers who were at Paris and Rambouillet from his days as an ambassador and as a foreign minister. In addition, he had worked closely with Ambassador Hill during the Dayton process which ended the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Trial Chamber will hear the evidence of Mr. Zivota Cosic, who was the minister of mining and energy in Serbia in 1999. His ministry was responsible for electrical energy and the oil industry in the Republic of Serbia. When the war began in March 1999, Mr. Cosic was a member of the task force established to remove and relocate chemical and hazardous materials which were vulnerable to NATO bombing. These dangerous products were located close to densely populated areas and big cities in Serbia. And this relocation was necessary in order to avoid human and ecological disaster in event of a bomb striking one of these locations. You will hear that Mr. Cosic was in contact with Mr. Milutinovic every second or third day regarding these matters and that he sent him daily progress reports on this operation. The evidence will be that civilian authorities had not planned for a war, they were not prepared for a war. The authorities worked frantically to move these hazardous materials out of harms way from NATO air-strikes. Mr. Milutinovic worked on these matters, he worked to avoid disaster, and alleviate human suffering. You will also hear the evidence of Mr. Jovan Kojic, who in 1998 and 1999 was a member of the office of the president of the Republic of Serbia. Mr. Kojic was an assistant to Mr. Milutinovic's principal secretary, and he was primarily responsible for assisting the daily administration of the office of the president. He will testify about meetings which took place in Mr. Milutinovic's office, documents received by the office of the president, and the daily schedule and work routine of Mr. Milutinovic. The Chamber will hear evidence about a meeting between -- or meetings between Mr. Milutinovic and the late Dr. Ibrahim Rugova in April 1999 and, in particular, the meeting that took place on the 28th of April, 1999, in Pristina where the two men signed a joint declaration and addressed the media and they called for an immediate end to hostilities in Kosovo and Metohija and the resumption of talks with an aim of achieving an agreement on substantial autonomy and self-governance in the province. We say this is yet another example of Mr. Milutinovic working for the good of all citizens of Serbia, seeking political, peaceful solution through dialogue. And during the period of the war May to June 1999, Mr. Milutinovic never exercised any sort of power or command or control or giving orders or direction to any military, police, or security forces. Mr. Milutinovic never demonstrated any criminal intent or criminal conduct. Indeed, his acts and conduct and state of mind are quite the opposite of those alleged by the Prosecution. And the Trial Chamber will hear evidence about the events following the election of Dr. Vojislav Kostunica as president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the crisis which occurred in the country in October 2000. You will hear about the significant measures taken by Mr. Milutinovic at that time, at risk to himself and his family, to avoid tremendous violence in Serbia and to ensure a smooth democratic transition. We say this is yet another example of his overall character and personality. In the end, Your Honour, we say that Mr. Milutinovic is a person who is not capable of committing the offences with which he is charged. Throughout his life he never demonstrated any intolerance, extremism, hatred, or propensity for violence or the use of violence. This can be seen through his conduct and through his words. He is a man who has always sought political solutions through dialogue and compromise. Mr. Milutinovic's conscience is clear. He has consistently rejected the allegations made against him by the Prosecution. He says the case against him is unfounded and very much misguided. Mr. Milutinovic believes that the evidence presented before this Trial Chamber will provide a full answer to the allegations against him and that you will acquit him. Mr. Milutinovic would now like to call his first witness: Professor Ratko Markovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for your opening speech, Mr. O'Sullivan, but there are a couple of matters that we need to deal with before you do call the first witness. The first of these is a motion recently received to amend the Rule 65 ter submission. Mr. Hannis, do you have anything to say on that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, only to object to it being late. However, the fact that this witness is probably going to testify for a few days makes it less of a problem for us than it might otherwise be and in some ways that particular submission is helpful in specifically identifying which exhibits go to which portions of his testimony. So in general I just want to have an objection to the late filing of those things, but other than that, no further comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall allow the 65 ter list to be submitted -- to be amended. The second matter is this, the Trial Chamber today received a 92 ter statement of Mr. Markovic. Now, I understand you're taking his evidence, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So perhaps you should deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We, as you know, require these statements to be tendered 48 hours in advance of the evidence of the witness. And where it's a weekend, without trying to split hairs on technical detail, it's pretty important that the Judges receive this before the close of business on the Friday. It's pretty useless to me to get this this morning. I know you may say to me it may be some time before you reach this, and I'll have time to read it tonight or -- but I think that's not an ideal way to proceed. So I draw that to your attention and to the attention of all Defence counsel at this stage, that we expect these statements to be in our hands at a time when it's realistic for us to have them to prepare before the witness gives his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, but it was simply no time. We have notified our friends from the Prosecution on Friday that we will be tendering this 92 ter statement on the facts, and it basically consists of just a list of the documents which we intend to use with Professor and the comments Professor made concerning these documents. We aim -- we aimed this 92 ter statement, Your Honours, for -- in order to save as much time as possible because we have 108 documents which will -- which will be basis of the fact testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I recognise all of that, Mr. Zecevic. The point, nevertheless, that we make is one that must be observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That completes these formalities. You now wish to call Professor Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, we have just two or three other formalities, if I may. We would -- we would need to make an oral application to amend the witness notification. It concerns the Exhibit P461, which is a joint declaration made by Mr. Milutinovic and late Dr. Rugova on the 28th of April, 1999, and Exhibit 1D60 which is a video-clip of these -- of this occasion. Professor Markovic was present, as you know, because both of these exhibits are -- have been shown to the -- before in this trial. It is entirely our oversight not to include these two exhibits in our witness notification, which was filed last Thursday, but we -- we, I hope, remedied that by advising the OTP by mail last Friday that we will be using these two -- one document and transcript of the video-clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that complete what you have to say or are there other matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is a another matter which consists of translational issue, we have an issue with the translation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please deal with that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, it came to our attention that P856, which is the FRY constitution and constitutional law of 1999, which we intend to use of course with our expert witness, the English translation of that document is -- includes only item number 1, so it's just the declaration of the -- of the constitution of 1992. So therefore, we will refer to the Exhibit 1D139 for the English translation of Exhibit P856. 1D139 is definitely the same -- the translation of the very same document and is in court in the e-court, and we had provided the hard copies -- actually for the Trial Chamber and for -- for our friends from the Office of the Prosecutor in two binders of all documents that this witness will rely to -- rely on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing else, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you have any comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We're not -- I'm not surprised that he's going to use P461 and 1D60 regarding the meeting with Rugova, so I have no problem with that. And I think it's a practical solution to use 1D139, which has the full translation. But I did have another question regarding translations. There are a number of Politika articles that are proposed to be shown to the witness. I understand he seemed to indicate he's read the articles, and they refresh his memory about events that he has personal knowledge of. So he's going to be talking about his personal knowledge but if the exhibits are going to be offered, then I need a translation because I haven't been able to read them. I don't have them in English. I don't know what they say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will not be willing to tender these Politikas, except the ones which have the translations already provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think if they do provide any meat for you, Mr. Hannis, you're going to have to find it by having them translated yourself. Well, we note what you say about P461 and 1D60 and it's easy to excuse the failure to include these in the witness notification and the overall circumstances, and there is no objection to you referring to them. As far as the constitution is concerned, again it makes sense to refer to 1D139. It still astonishes me that constitutional documents are so confused in this case. That remains the position. It's becoming clearer but not entirely clearer yet, and as far as the Politika articles are concerned we note that where you intend that they should be exhibited that they have been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So can we now hear from Professor Markovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have Professor Markovic in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Markovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor Markovic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, would you be so kind to tell us basic information concerning yourself, your full name, and your title so that we can have it for the record.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ratko Markovic. I'm a full-time professor at the law school at the University of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you speak English, don't you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I understand English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Before we proceed, should you need a break, should you feel that you are tired or feeling unwell, would you please inform the Trial Chamber about that so that we can take appropriate steps.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, would you please tell me, since when have you been teaching law at the law school in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I became full-time professor of constitutional law in 1984, and I have been also teaching administrative law since 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You wrote over 250 legal papers?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after graduation I started -- I embarked upon an academic career. I started as an assistant professor, and then in 1984 and 1985 I was elected full-time professor. And up until today, I have been involved in academic and scholarly work. I wrote two textbooks for the students of law school on constitutional law. So far one textbook on constitutional law was published in 11 editions and the other textbook on administrative law was published in two editions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, I would kindly ask you to slow down when speaking so that the interpreters can catch up with you. Thank you. Professor, you wrote an expert opinion for this trial which has to do with the powers and position of the president of the Republic of Serbia. In that paper you presented your views on these issues, and I suppose that these views were based on your scholarly work and views and that this reflects your independent scholarly opinion on these matters. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote this opinion, this report, precisely for this trial. I did my best to present in a concise manner without too many details a critical view of the constitutional institutions since 1974, especially certain opinions which became prevalent among scholars and which were more of a result of political and ideological views on these matters rather than an independent and academic treatment of these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, you have a binder with documents in front of you. The first document in the binder is your expert opinion. Would you please take a look at that. It is right in front of you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 1.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you wrote this document and reviewed it on a number of occasions recently. Is that the document right in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This document is marked as 1D682, and this is your expert opinion on the powers and position of the president of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, precisely so. The content of this opinion are consistent with the title because the work deals with the powers and position of the president of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, this work was based on your research of a certain number of laws and regulations, which are all listed in your statement dated the 30th of July, which we can see as tab 2 in this binder.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most of these documents have been quoted in my expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you gave this statement and you signed it on the 30th of July. It is marked as 1D745. Do you accept that this statement is true and correct to the best of your knowledge and that it contains all of the documents and regulations which you used in your expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the biography of the Professor Markovic is 1D684 and his bibliography is 1D683. We would move the Trial Chamber at this time to tender these four documents into the evidence, his expert report, bibliography and the 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, let us go back now to your expert opinion, tab 1 in the binder in front of you. Please tell me, Professor, your opinion focused on the analysis of constitutional provisions of the constitution of Serbia from 1990, which can be seen in tab 1 of this document. It is also marked as P855 and English translation is 1D139. You focused on Articles 83 through 89 in the chapter entitled "President of the Republic" as well as Article 132, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I also took into consideration the laws implementing these provisions wherever necessary, and also in issues where there was some constitutional practice I explained in footnotes what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your expert opinion in item 2.2, paragraph 2.2, you state that the powers of the president of Serbia are an exclusive constitutional category. Would you please elaborate on this position.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This is based on Article 83 of the constitution, on the last paragraph of that article, and it means that the powers of the president of the republic can be set forth only in the constitution and cannot be extended by legislation. This is a constitutional category in the sense that in that article of the constitution enlisting constitutional powers of the president cannot be expanded, nothing can be added to that article by legislation nor subtracted. This was the position also taken by the Constitutional Court of Serbia when they reviewed the constitutionality of the law on ranks of the members of the Ministry of the Interior. On that occasion, the Constitutional Court gave the same position, namely, that the powers of the president of the republic cannot be expanded by legislation; and for those reasons, those articles of the law which did that, namely, expanded on the powers, they were quashed or set aside by the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "Constitutional Court," you're referring to the Constitutional Court of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Later on we will go back to this issue dealing with the decision of the Constitutional Court of Serbia. Professor, would you please explain to the Chamber the importance of the 1990 Serbian constitution marked here as tab 5, P855 and translation at 1D139. Would you please explain the importance, the significance of that constitution.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Briefly speaking, it is dual, the significance. On the one hand it is an expression of the then-existing political constellation of the then-social -- of the then-socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia where the danger of secession of certain republics was quite imminent, and in order to avoid a situation where there would be a constitutional vacuum in Serbia, the Constitution of Serbia was passed in 1990, which provided the Republic of Serbia, even though it was still a federal unit, but nevertheless it provided attributes of an independent state to Serbia. This is one feature of this constitutional. And the other feature of the 1990 constitution is that it brought about a radical reform of the constitutional system, which in its depth had all features of a constitutional revolution. That is to say that new principles and new institutions were introduced which represented a break with the previous constitutional system. They introduced such categories as markets, private property, equality of all forms of property, multi-party system was introduced. In addition to that, they also introduced a mechanism for -- a mechanism of a parliamentary republic, that is to say they introduced a parliamentary form of government. They expanded the competency of the Constitutional Court, as well as the catalogue of human and civil rights. Instead of a commonal system they introduced local self role. This would briefly be what the reforms of the 1990 constitution were. Once again let me repeat that it introduced a radical break with the previous constitutional system, a radical departure from it, and this is why this constitution never uses a term "socialist."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. After the 1990 Constitution of Serbia on the 27th of April, 1992, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was created, and it was on that date that the constitution of the FRY was passed in 1992. You can see it in tab 6 in the binder in front of you. It is Exhibit P856. Professor, please tell us what were the legal consequences of the adoption of the 1992 FRY constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia from 1992 was adopted in order to provide a constitutional form for two republics, two federal units which did not secede from the Federation, those were the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro. The previous federal constitution from 1974 was created for a federation which had six federal units. Since four of them had seceded from the Federation, the remaining two formalised their union in the 1992 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The purpose of continuation of the Federation comprising two federal units was to preserve Yugoslavia as a subject, to preserve the legal personality of Yugoslavia and to formalise this union of the Republic of Serbia and Republic of Montenegro. This purpose is explained in the preamble of this 1992 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Please tell me, with the adoption of the FRY constitution, the one that we will be referring to as a federal constitution and on further examination there was an obligation for the constitutions of the two federal units as well as all federal legislation and republic legislation to be in compliance with the constitution. This is set out in Article 115, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a typical provision in every constitution, that the law of the federation constitutional -- federation constitution and federal legislation come above those of the federal units. This is a typical provision. In this case it is expressed in Article 115, which provides that the constitutions of the republics, as well as legislation of the member republics, as well as all legal regulations have to be in compliance with the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. This is an old maxim in fact dating back to the Swiss constitutional law, namely, that the federal legislation comes above those of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. In relation to the provisions of Article 115, would you please explain to the Trial Chamber and everybody else here why was it necessary to adopt the law on implementing the constitution and why was it necessary to bring all legislation in compliance with the constitution as well as why it was necessary to set aside certain legislation. If necessary, we can split this in three questions.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The meaning of the constitutional law is the same in all systems. Any constitutional law must regulate a transitional regime being used for a transition from an old system to a new system, and this is also the meaning behind this constitutional law which was adopted in order to have the 1992 constitution implemented. It goes without saying, in view of what we mentioned a while ago, the need for consistency between all federal and republican laws and provisions, the transformation between the two systems, the old and the new, must be gradual, the constitutional systems. Therefore, dates are determined or deadlines by which certain laws must be harmonized with the federal constitution. Also, deadlines are defined for certain laws to cease to have effect. This is the meaning of the constitutional law for implementation of the constitution. It provides for a smooth transition between the old system and the new, and this is something that is defined by the constitution which is to be implemented by the new constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In order to illustrate this point, could I please ask you to go to tab 7, Professor, this is 1D358. This is the constitutional law on the amendments to the constitutional law on the implementation of the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia in this specific case. Could you please comment on Article 1 and Article 4.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In Article 1 of this constitutional law, what we can see is -- is that a deadline is set of two years from the date of the amendment to the constitution, and then instead of this we have the following wording: "By the 31st of December, 1992, defined as the ultimate deadline for the harmonizing the laws with the new constitution, therefore, this deadline is hereby extended." We see the same thing being done in Article 4. It reads: "By the 31st of December, 1992, all the remaining republican laws shall be harmonized with the constitution that are not yet consistent with it, harmonizing the relations that do not fall under the constitutional competence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia." Therefore, we see another deadline extension at work here in a manner of speaking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on just a moment, Mr. Zecevic, until I follow this. I take it that in the reference to Article 4 of the constitution -- sorry, in relation to Article 4 that's referred to in the middle of the page, the word "until" is an inaccurate translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're referring to the -- to the Article 4 of the constitutional law and "until 31st December" is the accurate translation, it says: [Interpretation] "By the 31st of December" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What I think was translated in the answer given by the witness was "... by the 31st of December all the other republican laws," in other words that was a deadline and "until" does not make any sense in the context of a deadline. Now, is the word --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- is the word you used capable of being translated "by" as --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is a proper translation because it is a deadline, yes, and Professor can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that deals with that point. Going back, your earlier reference was to Article 3. Now, I -- is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I referred to Article 1 and Article 4 of the constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the copy I have starts with Article 3, and again the witness's answer did not fit the terms of Article 3 and that might make sense if he was referring to Article 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I just saw right now that the Article 1 has not been translated for some reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, now -- the position is now clear. That -- we've heard what the witness has to say about both Article 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And Article 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and Article 4 and we can move on --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- but it may be important -- it may be of course that the exhibit that is tab 7, in fact, includes Article 1, I don't know. But you should take steps I think to make sure that Article 1 is properly translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We will definitely do that. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the inconvenience. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, I think we have been successful in explaining the situation; however, I would just like to revise this now. When the constitution was adopted, certain laws were modified, or rather, adapted to fit the new constitution in order to bring them into balance with the constitutional provisions, whereas some other laws ceased to exist or have effect. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and if you look at the first constitutional law, that is probably the best example. The one on the implementation of the 1992 Constitution of the Republic of Serbia, this was published in Official Gazette number 1, dated 1990. All of the later constitutional laws amended the deadline by moving it, deferring it, as it were, since the original request proved to be overly ambitious and the deadline set too short for the harmonization process of all legislation and the new constitution to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Professor, what about illustrating a situation where certain regulations cease to have any effect whatsoever? We have tab 8, 1D370. Could you please have a look and comment, if you can, sir, on Article 1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] The translation is provided in the whole -- the whole law, Your Honours. It's tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just comment, if you can, please. I'm talking about Article 1, the very beginning of the article -- since it then goes on to list all these specific regulations that no longer apply.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Quite simply, what we see here are laws that cannot be harmonized with the new constitution by simple amendments. Instead, these need to be replaced by laws that are entirely new. There is a list here of 25 such laws listed one by one that now cease to apply. A special law was introduced and these ceased to apply, but this can only be determined by a new law. It is perhaps interesting if you look at item 7 that one of these laws that ceased to exist or apply is the law on the acts and conducts of republican organs in special situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We have explained in outline at least the situation surrounding the 1992 constitution and the 1990 constitution as well as the consequences; specifically, the constitutional laws that were passed for the implementation of this constitution as well as the legal consequences for any existing laws. I would now like to take you back to the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia. I'm talking about tab 5, P855, specifically Articles 83, 89 -- 83 and 89 as well as Article 132. Before we do that, sir, could you please tell us how you see the practice regarding the election of the president of Serbia, the appointment of the president of Serbia. What are the possible complications in relation to that, bearing in mind the time-period between 1997 and the present day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The election procedure itself, the way the president of the republic is appointed, is a complex one. According to the original wording on the law on the election of the president of the republic, an election is only valid if a majority of Serbia's voters go to the ballots, those that are listed on the electoral register. Therefore, this very complex condition had to be met in order for an election to take place and be valid. The winning candidate was the candidate who got the most votes. If there was no such result, the ballots were counted and then one had to go to the second round where the two most successful candidates from the first round ran. Eventually the one garnering the most votes was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, back in 1997 there were two elections, right, or rather, two rounds?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There were two presidential elections back in 1997. The first time around Mr. Lilic and Mr. Seselj ended up in the second round; however, the one universal condition was not met and that's why the election had to be done all over again. The new election took place and then Mr. Milan Milutinovic was elected president of the republic after round two of the election.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In 2002 Milutinovic ceased to be the president and there were three other elections taking place in Serbia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, two of which failed for this very reason, and then the electoral law was amended. The law on the election of the president of the republic was amended, and this condition was abolished, saying that a majority of the voters on the register must participate. It wasn't before then that the now-President of Serbia, Boris Tadic, was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 855 on the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 5, the Constitution of Serbia of 1990 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is a declaration on the promulgation of the constitution with the constitution attached. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the declaration of the -- of a promulgation of the constitution is the document which each and every time when the new constitution is taken, there is a declaration of -- on its promulgation. And then the actual text of the constitution is included in P855.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. I think we also have as the formal exhibit number for the FRY constitution P986.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the FRY constitution is P856 and the translation is 1D139. That is the document I was referring to at the beginning of my presentation, the one which doesn't have the proper translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we may have found the explanation for your difficulty about translation. In P856 you only have the one page translated, as you explained earlier --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and the constitution attached to it is in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the reason for that is probably that we have an exhibit which is the constitution, and that is P986. Now, I don't want you to interrupt by examining that issue now, but at the break you might wish to check that. Now, we're working on your 1D139 anyway for the moment but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- it's this sort of thing that can tend to cause confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know, Your Honours, but P986 is not the document from the Official Gazette, and that was the whole point. And when we -- when we stipulated earlier with our friends from the Prosecutor, we insisted that we stipulate only to the Official Gazette text. And somehow the problem was oversaw concerning the other translation of P856, which was in fact stipulated by the parties. Therefore, we have provided the translation which is 1D139.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have Exhibit P855, Article 83 displayed on the e-court, please. It's at tab number 5 in this binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, we have your expert opinion before us, and I'm looking at paragraph 2, 3. You say that all powers of the president of the republic can be divided into three groups, three types of powers, if you like, the first being representing the state of Serbia; secondly, those relating to the attribute of the president of the republic as non-operational executive; and the third being irregular situations. Can you explain based on which you envisaged these different types of groups of powers and when you say "representing," what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I have described these competences in groups. I have not listed each one of the 12 powers from Article 83, 84, 85, 89, and 132. Instead --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have on the e-court both pages because I see it's cut in half, the Article 83 is cut in half, so it's page 14 and page 15. If we can have both pages for the complete picture of the Article 83 to which Professor is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Professor, for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will solve that. It is apparently not possible. I'm really sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please continue -- [Interpretation] Please continue, Professor. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: So for the sake of better presenting the essential points, all the constitutional powers of the president are classified here in three groups. This is not to add anything or detract anything from the scope of the powers of the president of the republic. With reference to the first group, that is, the powers relating to representing the state of Serbia, this is a generic property or attribute of every head of state. The definition of a head of state, whether he be a monarch or the president of a republic, is that he or she personifies or represents the state. Therefore, as an organ representing the state as a whole, expressing the unity of the state, the president of the republic has the powers I have enumerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this second group of powers, the powers relating to the attribute of the president of the republic as a state organ representing a stable non-operational executive, what do you mean by non-operational executive?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Although according to Article 9, paragraph 2 of the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia, the president of the republic does not have executive power. In view of the powers he has, he is the closest to an executive organ. He does not have operational powers of executive power. The body that does have these powers is the government. For this reason, the president of the republic in this kind of constitutional order is a state organ representing non-operational executive. In other words, he does not have operational executive powers; rather, it is the government that has such powers. This second attribute is a consequence of a system of a government established in the constitution of 1990 and which is theoretically described as a mixed system of government because it combines the characteristics or some characteristics of a presidential system of government and a parliamentary system of government. Basically, this is a parliamentary system of government, but amended with some principles that are characteristic of a presidential system of government; primarily referring to the election of the president and not to his powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "in this," you mean in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm constantly referring to Serbia because you're asking me about the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now explain what this third group, the special powers relating to irregular situations refer to, and then we will take a break.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Irregular situations are situations which are not regular. It's a negative definition. These are situations in which there is a disruption between the legislative and executive power. Their relations are disrupted. The powers established in a regular state are disrupted. The scale or register of irregular circumstances according to the constitution of 1990 encompasses three states: A state of emergency, which is the lowest degree; then the state of an imminent threat of war; and finally, a state of war. The powers of the president of the republic, according to Article 83 or some of these powers, are linked to such irregular circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's about time to have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's also a suitable time --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If it pleases the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, but it's also a suitable time just to ask one question before we have that break. Professor, we've read your report and the theoretical situation is very clearly set out in that report. There's one gap I wonder if you could fill for me. It may be my fault that I missed it, but can you tell me who it is, apart from the position of prime minister, who it is that appoints ministers of the government in terms of this constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, candidates for minister are proposed by the prime minister designate, and the appointment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think I've -- that's a simple answer which I understand. I assumed that was the position, but I was anxious to be clear because I don't think it's spelled out in the constitution. Just one final matter before we part. I appreciate all you say in your report about checks and balances and the relationship between government, the National Assembly, and the president. But assuming that the National Assembly consists of a majority of members of the same party as the president, are the odds that the president's nominee who will also himself nominate the government ministers would be approved by the National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the simplest situation that can arise, if the majority in the National Assembly and the president who has been elected by a majority of the votes are both from the same political party. If the government, or rather, the majority of the National Assembly and the president come from the same political party, then it's almost certain that the prime minister designate and the -- proposed by the president of the republic and the candidates for minister proposed by the prime minister designate when there is a homogenous party majority -- however, we have a proportional system of proportional representation, and since it has existed and it has existed since the second parliamentary elections in the Republic of Serbia, there has never arisen a situation where there is a homogenous party majority in the national assembly. It's usually a coalition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I entirely understand that we have to look at the factual position and no doubt we'll get to that and it will be clarified. When were the second parliamentary elections in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second parliamentary elections were held in 1992. The first immediately after the constitution entered into force in 1990. In 1990 there was a majority system for seats in parliament to be distributed, and then the SPS has a homogenous majority. However, as of 1992 it hasn't had that majority --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the facts are a quite separate matter. At the moment we're looking at the theory, and you're looking at the terms of the constitution and it's in that connection I ask these questions. We'll move on to the factual position, no doubt, at a later stage. It's necessary now to have a break for various administrative reasons, and we will resume at 20 minutes past 11.00. Meanwhile, the usher will show you where to wait. Just please leave the courtroom now with the usher. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at 11.20.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before -- before we start, I'm sorry I omitted something this morning when I was referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- when I was referring to our amendments to 65 ter, we wanted to amend the 65 ter concerning the Exhibit 1D752, which is Article 56 of the Federal Republic of Germany basic law or constitution 49 of 90, the oath of office. And I'm sorry I omitted to mention that this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The OTP was advised by e-mail on Friday about that and this oath will be used during Professor's expert testimony, as Professor would like to explain through it the legal nature of the oath which is provided for in the Constitution of Serbia. I talked to my friend Mr. Hannis, and he assured me that he doesn't object to this. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall allow you to do that, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, and I'm really sorry for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue with your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have prepared a PowerPoint presentation for -- for the purposes of clarity of the issues we are going to talk about, and it refers to the Article 83 of the Serbian constitution and the competencies, powers, of the president of Serbia. And we have provided a copy to the registry, and we have three of these presentations. And it was suggested to us that we -- if it pleases the Court, that we take the IC numbers for each and every of the presentations with the number of slides included in that -- in that particular IC number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems a sensible way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Could we have the presentation number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC131, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is it -- I'm sorry. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, we have prepared this PowerPoint presentation and it will take place on the screen before you. As we proceed through the presentation, please comment page by page.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've been over this already, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's the -- that's the whole Article of 83 in the Constitution of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the witness has categorised these into three.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, three different -- three different groups of competences or powers of the president. Could we have page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, could you explain what this page is about, what does it show?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This page explains the legal status of the powers the president of the republic has according to Article 83. In some cases, he has no powers at all, later on I will explain why; in some he does have power to act; there are some powers he can exercise only upon agreement of the majority in the parliament; and there are some powers he cannot exercise because the appropriate legislation for the implementation of the constitution has not been adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So the colour red are powers that he has no possibility of exercising?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are powers which in every federal state in the world are reserved for the federal state. They are powers linked to the defence of the country and foreign policy. In view of the fact that the Constitution of Serbia, as I said, was adopted to prevent a constitutional vacuum should the Yugoslav Federation fall apart, it was drafted as if Serbia were an independent state. And that is the reason for such powers given to the president of the republic. However, according to Article 135 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come to that later. I do apologise for interrupting you. I only wanted to explain this colour code which is on our monitors. The colour green designates powers the president can exercise, blue marks powers the president can exercise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, what's the point in having a PowerPoint, then asking the witness to go over the four or five colours, and then doing it again yourself. I thought this was supposed to speed up and clarify things. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I thought that it wasn't explained by the colours. That was the whole point of my exercise. Could we have the next -- slide number 4, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, would you explain this to us now. This page shows the categories of powers, the three groups as you explained to us. In yellow we see the powers which the president has in order to represent the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In yellow we have here the powers relating to him being the head of state representing Serbia. In grey we have powers which the president has as a non-operational executive. And in this third colour, I don't know how to call it, we have the powers which president has in irregular situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the colour on the right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the colour on the right. I don't know how to clarify it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm obviously now going to struggle with the additional colours. I assume just for the moment that where it was red it was perhaps something he couldn't do, but are the red numbers here and the colours of the numbers of some significance?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm coming to this right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The numbers which we can see in these rectangles denote provisions of Article 83; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are actually all the constitutional powers of the president of the republic categorised pursuant to their legal status. Some are the powers that he cannot exercise, some he can exercise only upon an agreement of the parliament, and some powers can only be exercised by him at the proposal of another state organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now we're dealing with the powers enumerated in Article 83, paragraph 1, would you please comment on this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please go back to the previous one just for a moment and go back to the one before that. Right. Let's go forward one, please. So should we take the view that where the number is in red, that is something that the president could not do?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have the slide number 5, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, would you please explain this slide. This is Article 83, paragraph 1, marked in blue. Would you please explain why is this so.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In the enumeration of the powers of the president of the republic, this is the first power; namely, to propose a candidate to the National Assembly, a candidate for the post of prime minister upon hearing the opinion of the representative of the majority in the National Assembly. The president cannot exercise this power on his own because the candidate -- the identity of the candidate is opposed by him as a result of the elections, and he has to go with the person proposed by the majority in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, this is Article 83, paragraph 2. This one is in blue as well. Would you please give another brief comment.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the power of the president to propose candidates for the president and judges of the Constitutional Court. Once again, he cannot exercise this power either without abiding by the opinion of the parliamentary majority. He needs to previously reach an accord with the cabinet which personifies the parliamentary majority to see whether the candidates that he proposes can receive the majority of the votes in the Assembly. Recently we had a case where the current president of the republic gave his candidate for the president of the Constitutional Court without obtaining prior approval of the majority in the parliament, and this candidate was not confirmed by the Assembly. So in this case the presidential has to abide by the opinion of the parliamentary majority. He is not free to propose the candidate that he wants and the parliamentary majority does not approve.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see slide number 7, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
