utterances.text: This is Article 83, paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Again before you move on, the example you've just given, Professor, you're not saying that the president acted unconstitutionally, are you? Stupidly perhaps, but not unconstitutionally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the president can embark upon an adventure whereby he would propose a candidate without consulting the cabinet prior to that. If he wants his candidate to be appointed, he needs to consult the prime minister because only upon obtaining the support of the parliamentary majority, which he can obtain through the cabinet, will his candidate be appointed. If he's acting on his own without consulting the cabinet, then he risks his candidate not being appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I -- I understand that and I am simply making the point it means what it says. So why do we have to labour all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we want to show by this presentation we want to show that the limits of the competences of the president --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you don't think the report does that adequately?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You don't think the report, the expert opinion, does that adequately?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We're sure it does that adequately, we just wanted to be -- for the purposes of clarity and to be crystal clear in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is a limit to the extent to which we wish to be treated as school children.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. It wasn't our intention at all, Your Honours. We just -- I mean, if you don't -- if the Trial Chamber would not like us to proceed with this presentation we can come to -- we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suspect you're coming to more interesting examples and therefore I won't stop you for that, but please skip over the ones that really state the, as we say, bleeding obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just wanted to show the completeness of the whole. Thank you. Can we have slide number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Article 83, paragraph 3. Would you please explain very briefly why this one is in blue as well.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Because the promulgation of laws has to do with the adoption of laws in the Assembly. The president can promulgate only those laws which were adopted in the procedure prescribed in the Assembly. So this promulgation is not an independent act of the president; it has to do with a constitutive act, the adoption of law; whereas, the promulgation itself is a decorative act. The President simply states that what bears the title of a law is indeed a law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we move to number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is Article 83, paragraph 4 of the Constitution of Serbia, it is in red. So in your opinion this is a power that the president cannot exercise?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not that it's my opinion. It is based on the principle of relations between the federal constitution and that of Serbia. This is based on Article 77 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, this is something that falls within the jurisdiction of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, this led to a law on ministries, under which there were ministries established, I think three in all, for foreign relations, for international aid I think, and I can't remember what the third one is offhand. Were these ministries ever established in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those ministries were established and those were the Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and Ministry for Economic Relations with Foreign Countries. However, when the first review of the Law on Ministries was conducted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I know that from your report, but if all that was being done here was to create formally a situation which could be implemented if Yugoslavia fragmented further, why did the ministries actually have to be established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had to be established so that Serbia, who "volens nolens" wouldn't become an independent state should there be a total fragmentation of Yugoslavia, be given all instruments of statehood so that it would have its minister of defence, its minister of foreign affairs. Because as a member of a federation it was not entitled to have such ministries because these are the matters that fall within the jurisdiction of the Federation; and this was a transitional period of time. Those ministries existed for a brief period of time only because the first government of the Republic of Serbia pursuant to the 1990 constitution was set up in late 1990 or perhaps early 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think that does explain the position, Mr. Zecevic, but please continue. Perhaps it will be clear later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have slide number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, this is Article 83, paragraph 5, once again it's in red, so this must be one of the powers that the president cannot exercise. A brief explanation, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: As in the previous case the same explanation follows here. Serbia did not have armed forces, did not have its own army, and defence did not fall in -- within the jurisdiction of Serbia. The defence matters were within the jurisdiction of the Federation, and the Federation had the Army of Yugoslavia. So this was a power that the president of the republic could not exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is Article 83, paragraph 6. Would an identical explanation apply in this case as well, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All of these irregular situations, meaning state of emergency, state of war, and state of an imminent threat of war, fell within the jurisdiction of the federation, namely, the Federal Assembly and federal cabinet. This is why the president of the Republic of Serbia could not exercise this power.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is slide 11, Article 83, paragraph 7. It is in red colour, denoting a power that the president cannot exercise. Would you please explain.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This is the power of the president of the republic to adopt instruments or enactments that regulate matters falling within the competence of the National Assembly or only during a state of war or imminent threat of war. So only under those two types of irregular circumstances. As soon as they cease to exist, the president is duty-bound to present those enactments to the Assembly for confirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, let us spend some time here. I'm sure that the president -- that the Trial Chamber would be interested in this. It is a fact that President Milutinovic during the state of war which lasted from the 23rd of March, 1999, until the 10th of June, 1999, adopted a certain number of decrees, namely, 16 of them which are based on this article. In this presentation you categorise this as a power that should be marked red. Would you explain this, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: That's because he is not the state organ that declared the state of war or the state of an imminent threat of war. Initially it was done by the national assembly, and in cases where national assembly cannot be mean it is done by the federal cabinet. The president under those circumstances adopts these enactments at the proposal of the cabinet because they fall within the jurisdiction of the National Assembly. The federal cabinet and the federal president cannot pass enactments that fall within the jurisdiction of a federal unit. That was the reason why the president of Serbia adopted these enactment under those circumstances because these are the enactments pursuant to the Constitution of Serbia. These matters fall within the jurisdiction of the Republic of Serbia in this particular case within the jurisdiction of the National Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm -- it may well be me, but I'm not understanding this very clearly. I thought that this power was a federal power. Have I misunderstood that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Actually what -- if -- Professor can -- would you like Professor to answer this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Declaring a state of war and a state of an imminent threat of war is something that falls within the jurisdiction of the Federation. Under those circumstances, the federal cabinet adopts enactments that fall within the jurisdiction of the Federal Assembly, but here we're dealing with the responsibility of the republic, the competency of the republic, under Article 72 of the Constitution of Serbia. This is a competence that belongs to the National Assembly of Serbia. It says here that the president adopts these enactments only if they fall within the jurisdiction of the National Assembly, which is specified in Article 73 of the constitution. So this is not something that falls within the federal jurisdiction, even under federal constitution, no. This is an issue that falls within the jurisdiction of a federal unit, that is to say Serbia. The same article is contained in the Constitution of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I now understand that, but I question why the colour is red now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Professor explained but he can do it again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Red is something there is no power to do according to your initial scheme, but here we have a constitutional provision that enables him to deal with matters within the jurisdiction of the Republic of Serbia during a state of war. That shouldn't be red, should it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is most likely because he himself did not declare a state of war or a state of an imminent threat of war; that was done by a federal organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But Article 83, 7 doesn't depend on the president making the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it's a matter of how you qualify it, but the essence in my mind is clear, the substance is clear. This irregular state of affairs is declared by the Federation, and once it's done when it comes to all the matters falling within the jurisdiction of the National Assembly, which is quite a large body with over 200 members, in that case the enactments which fall within the jurisdiction of the National Assembly are adopted by the president at the proposal of the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can try to offer some assistance to the Trial Chamber. Professor, if we look at Article 83, paragraph 7 of the constitution, this is a power that can only be exercised under so-called irregular circumstances, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You are saying that these irregular circumstances need to be declared by the federal bodies and not the republican bodies, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is precisely what the constitution says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Article 83, paragraph 7 is marked in red precisely because the federal bodies must create circumstances for this to be applied to begin with, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is no spontaneous application, so to speak, without this first being rubber-stamped by a federal body.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, please, there's one thing I would like to ask you. Before you start answering make a short break so that the interpreters have a sufficient time to catch up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Number 8, please -- slide number 12, article -- [Interpretation] Article 83, paragraph 8 of the constitution, also marked in red.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain why, Professor, briefly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The same explanation applies as that which applies to the previous paragraphs, talking about the competence of the Republic of Serbia in cases where it is an independent state. But for as long as it remains a federal unit, this falls under the jurisdiction of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Finally we come to a green one. Can you please explain, Professor, briefly what this is about, Article 83, paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a power that the president has as a chief of state; however, this complex procedure and granting pardons is not something that the president does on his own and simply of his own accord. The first thing that needs to happen is for him to provide an opinion on a pardon and submit it to a first-instance court, the court issuing a ruling or a judgement. The next thing that happens is this goes to the Ministry of Justice. It is not before all these have been implemented, all these steps, that the president can grant pardon. Formally he can't propose someone to be pardoned. Pardon needs to be requested or it can be granted ex officio. Ex officio in this case would mean the minister of justice and then he can initiate proceedings for a pardon to be granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Slide number 14, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This slide is in relation to Article 83, paragraph 10 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you move on in relation to 9 in Serbia are pardons, as they are in other countries, very, very unusual events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not sit on the pardon board or commission myself; therefore, I don't know how frequent a case this was. But it certainly is an exceptional thing of quasi-judicial competence, that's what we term it in practice, that's what it is for the president of the republic. And this is only ever done if the actual pardon is requested by a third party. I'm not entirely certain how this works in practice because I don't have all the relevant information at my finger-tips.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slide 14, please, Article 83, paragraph 10 marked in purple.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In order to have this power exercised, we need to have a law that was never passed, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The president could never exercise this particular power simply because the law on decorations and awards was never passed in Serbia throughout the time that the 1990 constitution implied. Therefore, only the federal president, the president of the federal republic, was in a position to exercise this power. Even as we speak, Serbia does not have this sort of law. The now-president of Serbia cannot exercise this right stemming from the 2006 constitution for the simple reason that no law has yet been adopted for decorations and awards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slide number 15, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is Article 83, paragraph 11, marked in green, as we see, which would mean that the president is in a position to exercise this power, is entitled to exercise this power, briefly, Professor, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This power is self-explanatory. The president is the sole executive, but in order to exercise a certain power he needs assistance. This assistance is provided by a range of technical services and bodies that he sets up himself. However, he needs to mind the budget that is at the president's disposal. So there are certain realistic limits in terms of setting up these technical teams and services. He cannot set up too many of those if the funds within the presidential budget happen to be limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you meant to say this. Your answer to that question started with: "This power is self-explanatory. The president is the sole executive ..." Did you mean to say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The word used by professor is "inokosan." It should be -- let me just consult. It is a -- [Interpretation] It's an independent organ.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only one, sole, individual, the constitutional provision from Article 9 applies. He's not the bearer of executive power. According to Article 9 of the constitution, this is for the government; however, the president of the republic is a physical individual. This is not a collegium of persons, it's not a board or body, that's why I used the term "sole" or "individual."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have slide number 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you have Article 83, paragraph 12 in front of you marked in green. Can you just please briefly comment on this.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This is something that we've spoken about already, the powers of the president is a constitutional category, and he can only exercise those powers listed in this article or other articles of the constitution. His powers cannot be established by the legislation nor can his constitutional powers be modified by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, having followed this presentation I am quite certain that we owe the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we please have slide number 4 on the ELMO, just for future reference. Thank you very much. Thank you very, very much. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, as I said, I think we owe the Trial Chamber an explanation in terms of what you mean when you say "reserve competences," meaning the powers that we marked in red for the purposes of our presentation. What about the influence of Article 135 of the Constitution of Serbia on your explanation and your specific position regarding this?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a peculiarity of the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia. In order to interpret it, one must bear in mind the historical background of the time when it was passed. I said something about this in answer to your first question, therefore I don't believe there's any need to repeat this now. We are looking at powers that if they happen to be in the jurisdiction of the federal state, must be implemented by the Federation according to its own constitution. Given the fact, however, that the Federation was in a state of disarray and was beginning to disintegrate, the 1990 constitution was passed in order to avoid leaving Serbia in a constitutional vacuum with solutions at its disposal that it needed and that any state in a situation like that would have needed. The 1990 constitution granted those powers to the Republic of Serbia, powers not normally granted to a federation within a federal state -- the federation within a federal state. Since the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia came about and the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was transformed into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the powers were given to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and that's why the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia had to be consistent with the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Hence, the state bodies of the Republic of Serbia were in no position to exercise powers that under the federal constitution were reserved for the federal state. And that is why these powers are normally termed federal powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, where is Article 135 referred to in the expert opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just bear with me, Your Honour, one second. 230, 2-3-0, paragraph 2-3-0.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. That deals with part of it. Are you -- Professor, is Article 135 insofar as it relates to provisions of other constitutions which might violate the equality of Serbia or threaten its interests a regular feature of constitutions of the constituent parts of a federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It is not usual for the constitution of a federal unit to talk about the same powers as the federal constitution, but it is no normal situation for a federation to disintegrate into its own federal units. This started happening at the time when the 1990 constitution was passed. This is a response to what you might say was an exceptional situation, and this provision is certainly not typical of the constitutions of the federal units. However, we need to know that this was a federation beginning to disintegrate into its component parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In 1990, did this constitution require the approval of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't necessary. Under the constitution then in force, which was the 1974 constitution, the federal units, that is, the republics, had the right to self-organise, meaning to use their own constitutions to regulate their own constitutional systems. However, these constitutions under the 1974 constitution had to be consistent with the federal constitution and not run counter to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you say that this provision, the second paragraph of this provision, was consistent with the federal constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not the first and not the second. However, this is an irregular situation. The Republic of Croatia passed its own constitution right after this, and again this new Croatian constitution was not consistent with the constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia either. The situation at the time was irregular, was abnormal, if you like, and it certainly wasn't typical of what things usually worked like in a federal state. This was a federation on the brink of break-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under the circumstances that prevailed at the time - and what I mean is the new constitution being adopted and all the provisions that we've been looking at - what Serbia really wanted was to protect its own vital interests, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The -- Article 135 in its entirety has the function to protect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have Article 135 from the e-court, please? It's tab 5, P855 and page number 6 -- 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, in your report at 2.6, and particularly in footnote number 6, you explain the substance of Article 135 of the Constitution of Serbia. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite correct. What you find here is the explanation of the purpose and the raison d'etre, if you like, of Article 135 in the constitution of a federal unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us try to simplify matters to the greatest extent possible. In 1990 constitution and the government provisions were adopted by Serbia in a bid to protect its own vital interests. One must bear in mind, however, that Serbia had no intention of leaving the federation of which it was then part and that was the reason why Article 135 was introduced. This article enabled Serbia to have certain powers should the federation begin to dissolve, while at the same time remaining within that federation and continuing to function as its member republic, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is precisely the meaning behind this. I addressed this a while ago. This is for Serbia to have at its disposal the instruments of statehood should a case of total overall dissolution occur, should the Federation break-up into its six component parts or republics all aspiring to become independent states.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. This provision of the constitution of Serbia in 1990 enabled the supremacy as you said of the federal constitution from 1974, I'm referring to the constitution of the SFRY in tab 9 here, P1623, and then as of the 27th of April, 1992, the supremacy was granted to the Constitution of the FRY in tab 6, that's P856, and then after that from 2003 it was the Constitutional Charter of Serbia and Montenegro which is here in tab 10. Is that correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This article was supposed to express the loyalty of Serbia to the Federation, to the federal state. Serbia in its constitution did not take for itself anything that was within the competence of the federal state; on the contrary, in Article 135 it says that everything that is within the competence of the federal state and simultaneously of the Republic of Serbia based on its constitution of 1990 will be done by the federal state in line with its constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because Serbia gave these powers to its organs in the constitution of 1990, these powers were simply a reserve in a manner of speaking and that is why you termed these provisions reserve powers?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are powers in case Serbia became an independent state. That's why they are referred to as reserve powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And Serbia became independent only in 2006?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that was when this constitution was replaced by a new one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I think that for the sake of completeness and clarity we should illustrate these situations. You gave more explanations in paragraphs 2.5 to 2.10 of your paper, but now I would like to ask you in order to comment on the relevant legislative provisions, would you please open tab 19, that's 1D750, the Law on Carrying out Foreign Affairs Tasks Within Competencies of Federal Administrative Organs and Organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have it on the -- it's not in the system? 1D750.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've been given an untranslated copy of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the translation -- it's one of the very few documents that the translation is still pending, but I -- I would suggest that we -- that the Professor or I could read just an article in it and it be translated by the translators --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, apparently the B/C/S version is in the system, so you can proceed the way you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, have you found it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is the law on exercising foreign affairs tasks within the competence of federal organs, and it's dated the 16th of October, 1981, so this was the law regulating foreign affairs during the existence of the former Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. Is that correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, and one can see that these are all tasks within the competence of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will read only Articles 3 and 5 which I think illustrate the situation. Article 3: "The federal administrative organ and federal organisations shall carry out foreign affairs tasks within the sphere of their competence" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Zecevic please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you're being asked to slow down, please. It's a problem, always a problem, when you're reading from something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought that it was on the e-court, so I thought that the translators can read it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you could go back then and read from where you reached which was: "Simply within the sphere of their competence ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] "Independently on the basis and within the framework of the Constitution of the SFRY, the federal laws, other federal regulations, and enactments of the Assembly of the SFRY and within the framework of the foreign policy established after the SFRY and international treaties, and they are responsible to the Assembly of the SFRY and the Federal Executive Council for the carrying out of these tasks in the areas for which it is established." And then Article 5: "The Federal Executive Council shall direct, determine the manner of cooperation, and supervise the work of federal administrative organs and federal organisations in the area of foreign affairs falling within the competence of these organs and organisations. In conducting foreign affairs within its sphere of competence, the federal administrative organs and federal organisations shall cooperate with each other."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, just a brief comment, please. This law and these provisions regulate foreign affairs, do they not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was the law of the Federation which was in force for a long time. It was in force until 1998, and it is evident from these articles that this is a function of the Federation. The matter of foreign affairs falls within the competence of the Federation. And the federal organs dealing with that are provided for. These are federal organs and organisations and the Federal Executive Council, which was actually the federal government in those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When the SFRY ceased to exist and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia came into existence, a Law on Foreign Affairs of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was enacted, that's tab 20, 1D246.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have a translation, Your Honours, of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, have you found it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this law succeeded the previous law, and it regulates foreign affairs and it is evident from this law that this is still within the competence of the federal state, and the federal state exercises these powers through its federal organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And because this is within the competence of the federal state, both in the course of the existence of the SFRY and later on in the FRY, this power in the Constitution of Serbia in Article 83, paragraph 4 is marked red in our PowerPoint presentation in accordance with Article 135 of the constitution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Professor, you seem to be having a technical problem with this binder --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If we need to change the binder, we would gladly do that. We have one. I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I suggest, Your Honours, that we proceed so we don't use the time. It should be on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will see it on the monitor, Professor, the documents I wish to discuss with you. Tab 17, 1D456, this is a Law on Ministries, Article 5. His Honour, Judge Bonomy, at the very beginning asked you about it. This is the Law on Ministries from 1991 of the Republic of Serbia, Article 5.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Article 5 lists the ministries. There is a total of 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, one is the Ministry of Defence; 2, Ministry of the Interior; and then we have the Ministry for International Relations and Economic Development, do we not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this is from 1991, and when asked by His Honour Judge Bonomy, you said that when this law was amended for the first time, and in our set of documents that's tab 18, 1D142, Article 5 again, this is a Law on Amendments to the Law on Ministries. This is dated the 30th of August, 1993, it amends the 1991 law. Do you see this, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And in Article 5 it says: "The following shall cease to function on the day this law enters into force: The Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry for Foreign Economic Relations and Commercial Development." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is precisely these ministries that shall cease to function. In the meantime Serbia and Montenegro organised themselves into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and according to its constitution these areas fell under the competence of the Federation which is why these three ministries ceased to exist, since their fields of activity were now within the competence of the federal state, that's defence, foreign affairs, and foreign economic relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the reason why this law was adopted is that in the meantime the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was established in April of 1992, and this new constitution specified that these matters would fall within the jurisdiction of the federal organs; as a result of that, these Serbian ministries ceased to exist?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, let us now go back to powers in irregular circumstances. In our PowerPoint presentation they were marked in red, they were on the right-hand side in slide 4. This is 131, IC131, and these are the powers enumerated in Article 83, paragraphs 5, 6, 7, and 8. Let us now go -- start with Article 83, paragraph 6, which deals with the power of the president to declare a state of emergency or some other kind of irregular state. The Constitution of Serbia which is marked as ID139 in Article 78, paragraph 3 says what, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just try to find it, 78, paragraph 3. In Article 78 of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia we see that the jurisdiction of the Federal Assembly is regulated. It also says that among other things the Assembly decides on the change of borders of Yugoslavia, it decides on war or peace, it declares the state of war, the state of an imminent threat of war, and a state of emergency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So all three kinds of irregular circumstances fall within the jurisdiction of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all three kinds of these irregular circumstances fall within the jurisdiction of the Federation, and it exercises that through the Federal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, that same constitution, the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Article 99, paragraph 10, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It deals with who is going to declare these irregular states if the Federal Assembly is unable to meet. Since a parliament of any country is a multi-member body, it is difficult to assemble them, it's difficult to achieve quorum, and under those circumstances the competency for declaring some kind of an irregular state falls within the federal cabinet. So in those circumstances, when the Federal Assembly is unable to meet, the federal cabinet, upon hearing the opinion of the president of the republic, meaning the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as well as the Speaker of the Parliament, declares one of the irregular circumstances. So this is an alternative in those cases where the Federal Assembly is unable to meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just for illustration purposes, tab 11, P1664, is -- have you found it, Professor, tab 11, which is P1664? This is the decision to proclaim a state of imminent threat of war, which is item 186 of the Official Gazette of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, dated March -- 23rd March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This decision is the application of the constitutional provision that I explained just now. So the Federal Assembly was unable to meet, the federal parliament was unable to meet, and the decision on proclaiming a state of imminent threat of war was adopted by the federal cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now, let us move to tab 13, which is P1311, where we have the decision to end the state of war dated the 25th of June, 1999. This is tab 13, decision to end the state of war, 25th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The decision was adopted by the Federal Assembly; it was able to meet, therefore. And it adopted this decision to end the state of war, which is the greatest level of irregular circumstances. They adopted a decision to end the state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So we have now shown two decisions: One to proclaim a state of an imminent threat of war adopted under one set of circumstances where that decision was adopted by the federal government pursuant to Article 99, paragraph 10 of the Constitution of FRY, that was one type of circumstances; and the other type of circumstances was when the Federal Assembly was able to meet and adopted this decision, and that was the situation regulated by Article 78, item 3 of the Constitution of FRY?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Precisely because of these provisions of the federal constitution, provisions of Article 83, paragraph 6 of the Constitution of Serbia is as we have said a reserve power that the president of the republic has pursuant to Article 135 of the constitution?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can see that he only had that power on paper. He had it pursuant to the Constitution of Serbia, but since that constitution had to be in compliance with the federal constitution and the federal constitution put this within the jurisdiction of the federal state to be exercised via the Federal Assembly and federal cabinet, then that was done precisely by the Federal Assembly and federal cabinet and not by the president of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us move on. The president of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do that, the same I think applies to number 8 of the powers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But not to 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I was just starting with the 7, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, 7 was a power which actually was exercised. We've had that evidence. We know the details of that and what he said earlier, and I think also from the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is a fact. But we would just like to explain the mechanism, how the decrees were taken, Your Honour, during the 78 days of bombardment in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the power that we have already commented upon from Article 83, paragraph 7, is the power for the president to adopt decrees when the National Assembly is not able to meet in the -- is in one of the irregular circumstances. We have already discussed that, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And we said that those irregular circumstances occur as something that is beyond the control of the president of Serbia and the Assembly of Serbia because that falls within the jurisdiction of the Federal Assembly and federal cabinet?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So it is the federal organs that declare one of irregular state of affairs, and only after they do that does this power from Article 83, paragraph 7 could be possibly exercised, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this constitution was designed in such a way that they believed that either the National Assembly or the president, as specified by Article 83, paragraph 6, would be the one to declare this type of irregular state of affairs. And this is why this power was enumerated here. However, since under the federal constitution this falls within the jurisdiction of the Federation to be exercised either by the Federal Assembly or the federal cabinet, this possibility remain in Article 83, paragraph 7, whereby the president of the republic at the proposal of the cabinet could adopt enactments that fall within the competence of the National Assembly. The Federation cannot substitute the organs of one of the federal units because they remain even under the irregular state of affairs. However, this particular kind of irregular state of affairs was declared by the Federation through one of its organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is very repetitive, Mr. Zecevic, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was about that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- we're about to take a break, and I think we can take it now. One of the reasons for having an expert report is to allow the parties and the Bench to read it, and in a state of familiarity with that report to hear any supplementary matters that need to be addressed by the witness. There's little point in constantly repeating material which is in the report itself. Indeed, there's much to be said for getting to the stage of cross-examination on this as quickly as possible to see how much is really an issue. So we would welcome you directing attention to things you really need to ask supplementary questions about on constitutional matters rather than going over what is already there. We would also welcome copies of the PowerPoint slides in hard copy if you could arrange that for us at the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We will, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, we need to break again now for lunch, that will be for an hour, and we will resume at quarter to 2.00. So you should go again with the usher, and he'll show you where you should be during this break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll resume at 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.43 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, this is very helpful. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to express our gratitude to Riaz and the registry for helping us with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, were you able to have some rest? Were you, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: A bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will try to go at a slower pace.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You're quite welcome. In order to avoid repeating things, Professor, I decided to give you specific examples that have to do with powers from Article 83, paragraph 7 of the president. This has to do with decrees adopted in 1999, and we will briefly comment upon that. And should the Trial Chamber have some additional questions, then you will certainly provide explanations. While the state of war was in effect in 1999, President Milutinovic adopted a total of 16 decrees, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and all of them were published in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, all of these decrees were adopted at the proposal of the cabinet of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. All of them were adopted at the proposal of the cabinet, which formulated the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the text was sent to the president for him to sign it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the text was given to the president to sign, or rather, he was the one adopting the actual enactment, whereas the cabinet was the one who gave the content, who formulated the substance of the enactment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have tab 27, P993, second page, in Serbian; it's a decree on ID during the state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 27, Professor, page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, can we have the first page on e-court. It's the page number 6 of the English version, decree on identity cards during the state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, this Official Gazette number 17 is dated the 7th of April, 1999, contains four decrees which were adopted by the president in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: One of those decrees is the one on identity cards?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: During the state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. Professor, the law on identity cards is a republic law, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see tab 28, please, P183 ter, which is the Law on Identity Cards, dated the 13th of April, 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you found it, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Given that this was a republican legislation, it was the republican cabinet which submitted a proposal to the president to adopt a decree on identity cards during the state of war for the reasons that motivated the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This was done because this was a republican legislation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a law adopted by the republic on identity cards, so this is a legislation adopted by the National Assembly. But given that this was the state of war, the decree on identity cards regulated two situations. One is that the minimum age for identity cards was dropped from 18 to 14, and the other situation was the one where a person loses his or her identity cards and what needs to be done under those circumstances. So this decree regulated only these two situations, and this decree differs from the law on identity cards. But in this case the maximum lex specialis derogat legi generali was applied or the lex specialis dergogat legi inferiori, that one also applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in addition to this decree, there were another 15 decrees adopted by the president. All of those were decrees in relation to laws at the republic level, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: All those decrees were adopted with regard to questions within the remit of the National Assembly, it's a legislative competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The National Assembly, the People's Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- I need your help again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we're looking at, tab 28 --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- is a 1974 document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the changes that the Professor has just mentioned, these can be seen in the previous --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the previous tab, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's a decree on the Law of Identity Cards During the State of War.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All these other decrees are in the binders at tabs 29 through 41. Given the fact that they have been admitted already, there is no need to go through each and every one of them right now. In compliance with provisions of Article 43, paragraph 7, it is the president's duty once a state of war is over to submit these decrees to the People's Assembly for ratification, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A while ago we saw the decision of the Federal Assembly to declare the state of war over. Could you please go to tab 42, sir, 1D190 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you do that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- on the question of identity cards, do you know, Professor, why the rule on identity cards was changed? What was the purpose and what was to be achieved by this? I'm referring to the reporting of lost identity cards. I think I can easily understand the other one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under a state of war it is important to know the identity of a given person. Article 1 of the law shows or reads that an ID is a document proving a person's identity. It is precisely for that purpose in order to know who is who, so to speak, that the procedure was expedited for obtaining new IDs once an ID has been lost. Under a state of war - I'm no expert in the matter of course - but it is in the very nature of the situation that it is important to know who is who. Therefore, the expedited procedure for obtaining new ID, as compared to the regular procedure that applies in regular circumstances. If one loses an ID that doesn't mean that this person has lost his or her identity; you simply get a new one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was the consequence of not getting a new one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One can't really tell based on this law. This probably gives rise to a criminal report. There's probably more about that in the legal provisions governing the issuing of ID. This still applies if you don't have an ID on you and you happen to be ID'd by an official of the law, then a criminal report is filed against you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look at Article 18, I'm looking at it right now --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, Professor, I think the Judges are conferring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Professor wanted to give an additional explanation, and I cut him short because you were discussing something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Certainly, Professor, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 18 provides for this sort of situation. A fine will be imposed, and any person failing to submit a request to have a new ID issued to them by a certain deadline, this includes those who failed to declare the loss of ID by a given deadline and request a new identification document to be issued. Article 12 talks about what happens when people lose their identity papers. Article 18 contains incriminations in relation to this issue of IDs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one transcript correction. The Professor said -- yeah, it's page 78, 15, Professor said a report is filed, but it's the misdemeanour's report. It's not the criminal report. Professor used the word "prekrsaj" which is the misdemeanour not the criminal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As we said, Article 83, paragraph 7 says that once a state of war has been declared over, the president is duty-bound to submit these regulations for ratification?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please now go to tab 42, 1D190. Tab 42, 42, sir, it's a letter by Mr. Milutinovic to the chairman of the People's Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, Mr. Dragan Topic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: What he does here is perfectly consistent with the existing constitution, the constitutional norm. Article 83, paragraph 7 we've provided an explanation about that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the date on the letter is the 25th of June, whereas we said a while ago - and you can see that at the end of this letter - that on the 24th of June the decision to declare the state of war over had been adopted, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that means that the very next day the president of the republic sent this accompanying letter to the chairman of the People's Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, again 80, row 5, on the 24th of June the decision to cessation of the state of war has been adopted, not the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to tab 43, the next one please, 1D192, is the Law on Confirming the Decrees Adopted by the President During the State of War.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, here the parliament, the People's Assembly, takes action in compliance with Article 83, paragraph 7. If we look at Article 2, we see that some of these decrees are mentioned, there is a list which decrees exactly, and when they were abolished on which date, when these decrees ceased to have effect on a particular date, for example. Some of the decrees from the list are abolished on the day of adoption of this new law. Three different regimes are envisaged here in relation to the specific dates when the decrees will cease to have effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now yet another power - I don't want to repeat myself but I think this is very important for the course of our examination - this is the power under Article 83, paragraph 5 of the constitution. This is another reserve competence. This is clearly within the competence of the federal state. For that reason I would like to ask you to comment on paragraphs 99.9 and 135 of the Constitution of the SFRY -- of the FRY. This is tab 5, 586, and the translation is D139. Article 135 in relation to the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Article 99.9 in relation to the federal government.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Article 135 says that the Republic of Serbia has no armed force at its disposal, no army. The army is at the command of the Federation. This is the meaning of Article 135. Other than that there are three things being envisaged in the article: Who is in command of the army, being the first among these; the composition of these bodies being the next, the Supreme Defence Council; and thirdly, who presides over the work of this body. Article 89, I'm not sure which paragraph you mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It says that it is the federal cabinet or the federal government that orders general mobilisation and organises preparations for defence, which means that this is not something that is within the remit of the president of the Republic of Serbia, either at least under Article 83, paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, we shall now briefly address Article 83, paragraph 1 of the Constitution of Serbia. This is something you've explained already in quite some detail, I think, especially when you talked about the inability of the president to take such decisions independently without consulting the parliament -- parliamentary majority. I would like to ask you to comment on one thing that we came across at one point in time. Theoretically speaking, should the president appoint the president designate to head the cabinet, someone not enjoying the support of the majority, what sort of situation would that constitute in your opinion, the prime minister designate, that is?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: He should know that a designate like that cannot draw the parliamentary majority. So the only possible interpretation would be that he is obstructing the establishment of a cabinet, thereby violating the constitution. Any violation of the constitution is grounds enough to recall a president of the republic or to revoke him. This person does not enjoy the support of the parliamentary majority, and yet the president is opening this avenue to him that he should establish the set-up and the composition of the cabinet, thereby unduly influencing the work of the future cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We had a situation like that in Serbia quite recently. It was something along these lines. Could you please shed some light on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: It was similar to the extent that they had a great difficulty putting together a coalition, a political coalition within the Assembly, a majority you might say. As soon as there was a majority to speak of, on the eve of the expiry of the constitutional deadline, he -- the president did eventually appoint prime minister designate, thereby garnering the necessary majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What I had in mind, sir, was the fact that the president of Serbia, Tadic, who is the president of the democratic party, despite the fact that the democratic party had nominated Mr. Djeric, failed to offer the position to the candidate from the ranks of his own party. But rather he offered it to a candidate who enjoyed the support of the majority, the parliamentary majority, just to illustrate the situation, that's my intention?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely the position. It was not offered to a candidate from his own party but rather from a different one because that candidate had been successful in garnering the support of the majority in parliament. As we said, he is bound by the result of the parliamentary elections, and certainly he's bound by the parliamentary coalition and the parties constituting that coalition. He's bound by their positions and opinions. He's not at liberty to appoint or nominate candidates to the cabinet as he sees fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Professor. Just to avoid repetition, similar things apply to Article 83, paragraph 2, when it comes to appointing candidates to become judges of the Constitutional Court, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I've just provided an example for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's all right. Professor, I think there is one thing that we need to explain to the Chamber, and it's about the powers of the president under Article 83, paragraph 3, where he propagates laws by decree. The reason being in our own legal practice we have the distinction between "ukaz" and "uredba," ordinance and decree. In English the legal nature of these two is quite different. What we see here is that CLSS have decided to translate both by using the same word "decree," but could you please try to explain the difference between ukaz, u-k-a-z on the one hand as a legal enactment and uredba, u-r-e-d-b-a, on the other, as another type of legal enactment, u-r-e-d-b-a. It is for this purpose that we had prepared our next PowerPoint presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The PowerPoint presentation number 2, and if we can have the IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC132, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think usher can take away the previous presentation away, thank you very much, from the ELMO. And we don't need the -- thank you very much. Could we have the page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, you see the presentation on your screen, don't you, your left screen?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have page 2, please, slide 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, I apologise interrupting. I have certain confusions, and I thought Professor will very kindly help me out with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Now, I have seen Article 83.5 of the Serbian constitution, and I've also seen 99 of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the constitution. And according to the interpretation which has been given by the learned Professor and also the report -- in the report he has mentioned that the powers given under 83.5 of the Constitution of Serbia, the powers of the president of the Republic of Serbia is superseded because of Article 99 of FRY. Now, where does he get this from because as we -- as we compare constitutions, we find that usually there are lists of powers. There is the enafridgration [phoen], the federal unit has a list, the Federation has a list, and then there is also the concurrent list. Now, what I -- what I was understanding of 83.5 and 99 was as if these were concurrent jurisdictions. I shall feel very grateful if the Professor would kindly dilate on this. How does he say that 99 supersedes 83.5 of the Serbian constitution. And then I have an ancillary question later to ask. I'm very grateful for this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Thank you. As far as defence powers go, in Article 77 of the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia lists the powers of the federal state, the Federation. And in paragraph 7 it says defence and security of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So the subject matter of defence falls within the competence of the federal state, not the republic. As for control of the armed forces in peace and war, that's according to Article 135 of the constitution of the FRY, paragraph 1. It says that the Supreme Defence Council or the president of the republic has this power. But as for ordering a general or partial mobilisation according to Article 99, paragraph 9, this is within the competence of the federal government. Why are these provisions of the federal constitution valid here rather than the constitutions of the, or rather, the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia? Well, because of Article 115 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which says that the constitutions of the member republics have to be in harmony with or in conformity with the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So lex superior derogat inferoiori the federal constitution supersedes the constitution of Serbia as a federal unit of the Yugoslav federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: My second question would be -- of course these are two constitutions, one is of the federal unit, the other is of the Federation. Now, was this constitution of FRY adopted by Serbia or accepted in some terms and what were those terms? Did those terms spell out this sort of a relationship where concurrent powers are given? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both of the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro decided to associate themselves into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia by this constitution of 1982 -- 1992, and it says that it is the Republic of Serbia and the Republic of Montenegro, and that's in Article 2, which are the member republics. By associating into the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, both Serbia and Montenegro recognised the priority of federal law, that is, the federal constitution, federal law, and other federal legislation in relation to the law of each republic. Every federation in the world rests on such a law, the law of the priority of federal law over the law of the federal unit. That is the law of supremacy of the federal legal order in relation to federal units. This same rule applied to the Yugoslav Federation which existed until the year 2003, when it was transformed into a union and as of 2006, the 21st of May, 2006, the real union also ceased to exist, and in its place we now have two independent states: Serbia and Montenegro, both of which are independent and sovereign as of the 21st of May, 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Now professor, thank you very much. Now, one little more clarification coming from your learned self. Now, 99 of the FRY and 83.5, do you think there's a clash? Because both seem to be concurrent jurisdiction. There's no clash, it appears. How would you kindly help me get out of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both powers are identical when it comes to partial or total mobilisation, but Article 99 takes precedence over Article 83 because it is contained in the federal constitution. And the federal constitution takes supremacy over the constitutions of the republic members -- member republics, so that the -- the legislation which has a greater legal force invalidates the legislation which has a lower legal force. The Constitution of the Republic of Serbia says that it is the president of the republic who decides on mobilisation, whereas the federal constitution says that it is the federal government that makes this decision. As the rule is that the federal constitution takes precedence over the republican constitution, it follows that it is the government of the Federation which decides on the call for a general mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Professor, do you have any constitutional case on this point or is it your own interpretation, please? Any decision by the Constitutional Court on what you have said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for example, when the state of war was declared, we saw it was done by the federal government and not by the president of the republic. The same applies for mobilisation, both general and partial. So this is not my own personal interpretation, it is a federal rule. The federal constitution states that it supersedes the constitutions of the member republics, and when a situation arose where this had to be tested, it was the federal government which acted according to the federal constitution rather than the president of the republic. It was not the president of the republic who declared a state of imminent threat of war or a state of war, nor did he order general or partial mobilisation. All this was done by the federal government. So this is not my own personal interpretation; it is simply a matter of the mutual relationship of two pieces of legislation which are not equal in terms of legal strength, power. But we have not had any such cases before the Constitutional Court to date to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to clarify a point, Professor. To be quite clear, when in your previous response you said the president of the republic, you are referring to the president of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because there is also a federal president, so please pay attention to that when speaking. We have --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you wish me to pursue this issue anymore or you're satisfied with the answers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm most grateful. I just wanted to clarify some cobwebs to be removed. But as we go ahead, there may be more questions as we go through the text, but I'm grateful for the patience.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, thank you very much. At any time, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, please look at the monitor before you. We started --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, we need the PowerPoint again, the PowerPoint number 2, IC132, on the screen, slide number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, can you comment briefly on this slide. What does it represent?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember your question. You asked me what the legal difference was between these two words "ukaz" and "uredba," and the difference is many-fold. First of all, who issues the document, and "ukaz" can be issued exclusively by the president of the Republic of Serbia; and "uredba" is an enactment issued by the government. That's one basis to differentiate. The second basis is the content. Ukaz is a proclamation, it confirms a law and if so provided by the constitution it confirms that certain facts have arisen which have certain legal consequences. For example, the termination of the mandate of the Assembly by force of law or, for example, the president might issue an "ukaz" stating that the federal government has dissolved the Federal Assembly. That's in the constitution of 1992. Unlike "uredba," which is general enactment issued by the government and which execute legislation, they are connected to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, you said that an "ukaz" is exclusively issued by a president, the president?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In our legal system there is no possibility of any other state organ issuing an "ukaz."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As we see in slide number 2, there are two kinds of "ukaz," declarative enactments and constitutive act. Can you just explain briefly what the difference is between a declarative and a constitutive.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The difference is as follows. If an "ukaz" is a declarative act it simply states certain facts which have arisen, for example promulgating a law. It is simply established that the National Assembly in the legislative procedure adopted a law with the required majority. So the president of the republic issues an "ukaz" promulgating the law, the law when it is published or promulgated enters into force. That's an example of an "ukaz" as a declarative act. As a constitutive act, it's an individual act, something is being created by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just slow down, Professor, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: For example, at the federal level there was an ukaz on appointing an ambassador. Ambassadors and other diplomatic representatives are appointed by an "ukaz" or promoting someone to the rank of general, for example, or -- well, these are examples of the "ukaz" as constitutive acts which as a rule are individual acts. These are the two main types of "ukaz" existing in the legal system of our country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have slide number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slide number 3. There are three colours. Red designates the president of FRY, green the president of Serbia, and yellow the government or cabinet. Is that correct, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have slide number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, this slide refers to the types of "ukaz" issued by the president of the Republic of Serbia, which is why they are green?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. "Ukaz" or ordinance promulgating a law or ordinance on pardon and ordinance on promotion. In addition to this -- well, yes. You've put it here: Ukaz proclamation or ordinance. That's the explanation, the linguistic explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I said just some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is meant by ordinance on promotion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An ordinance on promotion was based on the law on ranks of members of Ministry of the Interior when the president of the republic, pursuant to this law and under the conditions provided for in the law, was able to promote someone to the rank of a general of the police, of the police force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where would the -- where would that power be set out in the first place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These powers are in the law on the ranks of the members of the Ministry of the Interior and as this law established a power not established by the Constitution of the Republic of Serbia in Article 83, that's precisely the situation I mentioned previously. The law extended the powers of the president that he has under the constitution, and for this reason the Constitutional Court declared this provision of the law unconstitutional and it was rendered null and void. Of course this was the Constitutional Court of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So although this power was exercised at some stage, it was unconstitutional and we could strike it off the bottom of this list, could we?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was declared unconstitutional, Your Honour, by the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, this is slide 5. These are the types of "ukaz" adopted by the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, this is why they are marked in red.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia has many more different types of "ukaz," given the competencies of the Federation. Since the Federation is a subject of international law and the Republic of Serbia is not, then the president of the federal state can issue "ukaz" to appoint ambassadors and diplomatic representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They are appointed to various posts?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, they are appointed to various posts, positions, pursuant to Article 135, for example, that of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or rather, I apologise, Article 136 of that constitution.
