According to it president -- federal president can appoint and dismiss officers of the federal army, president, judges of military courts, military prosecutors, all of this is done via "ukaz."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, let us just explain another matter. The key difference between the powers of the president of FRY and those of the president of Serbia when it comes to "ukaz" is that the president of FRY on the basis of the quoted article, Article 136 of the Constitution of FRY, can appoint and remove from office various individuals. No such -- the president of Serbia has no such powers, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The president of Serbia has only the power that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You meant the power to promote?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the power to promote. He has no power to appoint or remove from office. He can also issue an "ukaz" on awarding or decorating someone, given that at the level of the Federation there is a federal law on awards and decorations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, this could perhaps be an opportune moment to give some comments on what a promotion means in your view. What does an act on promotion mean, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: An act on promotion is an individual constitutive act when it comes to its nature. As to its content, its substance, it is synonymous with the word "promotion," it promotes someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can a certain individual to whom that enactment pertains be appointed to a certain position or can that person be given some powers via this enactment?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The president of the Republic of Serbia did not have such power, either on the basis of the constitution or on the law on the ranks of the members of the Ministry of the Interior. The Constitutional Court proclaimed the provisions that we mentioned unconstitutional; that is to say that the president could only promote somebody to a rank, but could not appoint or remove someone from office. Pursuant to the Constitution of Serbia, and I think that's in Article 90, it is only the Serbian cabinet or the Serbian government that can do that, that can appoint or remove someone from office, meaning the officials in the organs of the state administration. The president has no such powers. It is in Article 90, paragraph 5, where it says that it is the cabinet that appoints and removes from office officials in the ministries. Based on the Law on Ranks, the president could only promote somebody to a certain rank, but he could not appoint somebody to a ministry. No, that was something that only the Government of Serbia was entitled to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm rather confused by this now, Mr. Zecevic. Is the point now being made that, in fact, a rank could be awarded by the president but not a position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So where -- well, let me go back to Professor. Where is the power then to award a rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This power stems from the Law on Ranks of the members of the Ministry of the Interior, I think it's in Article 6 and 10 of that law. However, the Constitutional Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes -- I'm sorry, on you go --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Constitutional Court declared those articles to be unconstitutional, and thus they became invalid. That is to say that the Assembly adopted a law that had some unconstitutional provisions; it is something that happens in all countries, including the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So in the end of the day are you saying that the president of Serbia had no power either to appoint or dismiss someone from a ministry or to give them a rank or appoint them to a position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, president of Serbia was never even with that law on the ranks, was never given a power to appoint or dismiss, so that is completely out, and has never been one of his even unconstitutional competencies. Now, according to the Law on Ranks, he had the competence to promote, according to the law, which we will see later on, but that law was declared unconstitutional in these parts because, as Professor said at the very beginning, the rights, the competencies, and the powers of the president of Serbia derive -- derive only from the constitution. And it cannot be -- he cannot be awarded the competencies and the powers by law, and that was the reason why later this -- this law was declared -- declared unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court of Serbia. But at the time relevant to the indictment, this law was still in the full force, and that is why we have been -- it was declared unconstitutional only later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you go back to page 92, of line -- 92, line 23 of the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And line 24, in fact, the answer was: "The president of Serbia has only the power that I mentioned." And you then say: "You mean the power to promote?" And the answer was: "Yes." Now, what I'm understanding by all of this is that he didn't have the power to promote because the law that gave him that power was unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he had it during the time relevant to this indictment. He had it. It was declared unconstitutional only later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is the point of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So he thought he had the power?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he thought he had the power at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So is General Lukic a general or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is a general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He is. And was he created a general in this period?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He was promoted to a higher general post, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was that act unconstitutional eventually or constitutional?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, the powers of the president to do that has been declared unconstitutional, not the fact -- not the promotion itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So if he got it in in the time that the president misunderstood his powers, it's okay? Perhaps I understand that, now let's move on then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If Your Honour want me, I can consult the Professor on the issue and have the expert opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After all, I'm just a lawyer and lay person in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No it's consistent with the evidence now, but I was finding it confusing to think that if you have never had the power constitutionally, that anything you did could possibly be valid. I assume that normally when things are declared unconstitutional or enactments are -- everything that's happened under them is null and void, but you're saying that in Serbia a different practice was followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you comment on this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: A question would arise -- sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The decision of the Constitutional Court declaring the entire law or some of its provisions unconstitutional does not have retractive effect, does not have ex tunc effect, it has ex nunc effect. So the legal effects produced by an unconstitutional law or one of its provisions remain in force, they remain valid. It's just that in the future that law cannot be applied. This is the legal regime produced by a decision of a constitutional court, both at the level of the Federation while we still were a Federation, as well as at the level of the Republic of Serbia. In this new Constitution of Serbia from 2006, the same legal regime is applied, that is to say that the decision of the Constitutional Court did not have retractive effect that do not void the legal consequences produced by some unconstitutional provisions. It is just that their further application is made impossible. Thus, all the promotions which came about on the basis of that law by the president of the republic remain valid, even though later on the Constitutional Court declared those provisions to be unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: We are used to such declarations by the court. If something is ab initio void, then it is void. But then there are provisions which are remedial which means that the court protects those actions notwithstanding the fact that those provisions were void ab initio. Now, please be specific in helping us know whether the Constitutional Court protected those actions and notwithstanding the fact that they declared the law to be void or there was no protection. And if there was no protection how can they be valid? Was there a protection given in the judgement itself, sir? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Constitutional Court adopts decisions, not judgements. They adopt decisions, and the decisions of the Constitutional Court are of general effect, they are final, they are not appealable, and they are enforceable. So regardless of how it may seem from some other point of view, how illogical it may seem, this is how it was regulated in our legal system for as long as we have had a Constitutional Court. And we have had a Constitutional Court since 1963 in our country back in the times when we were a socialist country. And we were the only socialist country in the world who had a Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But who brought about the curing? I mean if the courts adjudicate, okay, or declare something that the powers were never there, then how did these acts that were so performed protected? There has to be either a court's order or a constitutional protection through a curative law or remedial law as we understand in the constitutional framework of laws?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't exist because the decisions of the Constitutional Court are final and are applied from that point on. They simply derogate an unconstitutional provision, they do not void it. This is our legal system. Our Constitutional Court, the Constitutional Court in the Republic of Serbia and earlier the one in Yugoslavia, was modelled after the German Constitutional Court and that in Austria and Italy. Those are three types of Constitutional Courts existing in Europe, and our Constitutional Court was modelled after them. Perhaps it's a bit difficult for someone coming from a different legal system to understand that, but this is how it is regulated in the European system of Constitutional Courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you well, Professor, our concept of Constitutional Courts is not something that is unique to Serbia only how -- on the contrary, it is modelled after the tradition of European Constitutional Courts?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We have adopted many solutions from these countries, even in our latest constitution, the one from 2006, we have used a lot of examples from the Constitutional Court of Italy. We modelled our current court after that one in Italy which had 15 members and the one now has nine. The authors of the constitution did not invent anything, no; they simply applied the practice existing in the continental law European countries with Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, now that we have touched upon this topic, in order to be of assistance to Their Honours in case they have some other questions about this decision of the Constitutional Court, I would like to ask you to look at tab 26 which is 1D639 [In English] 1D639. [Interpretation] This is precisely this decision of the Constitutional Court of Serbia, 26, tab 26. This is the decision of the Constitutional Court of Serbia that you referred to just a minute ago, if I'm not mistaken. Tab 26, 1D639.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have a complete translation. Perhaps you can comment on various parts of the decision. [In English] Appreciate that. [Interpretation] As I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The language appears clear that the challenge provisions shall cease to be valid, and that would presuppose that they had been valid. I think what Judge Chowhan was seeking was the basis for that sort of determination when it's something as fundamental as a breach of the constitution. And it may be that that's something you can think about and deal with tomorrow and we can proceed perhaps with something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, let's go back to our PowerPoint presentation, IC132, slide number 6, please. All right. Now we come to "uredba." "Uredba," or decree, as you have suggested, is an act within the sole competence of the cabinet; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. "Uredba," decree, is an enactment related to the enactment. A law has to do with the people's assembly, with the parliament, decree has to do with the government or the cabinet; and "ukaz," an ordinance or a proclamation is something that is related to the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at this slide we see that a decree is a constitutive act, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the legal system of the Republic of Serbia and the substance remains the same within the legal system of the Federation total, a decree is purely executive. You cannot use a decree without previously regulating a matter by law, change any -- or enforce any changes to the social relations. A decree must invoke a certain law or the provisions of a certain law for the implementation of which it is adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With the -- with one single exception, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is one exception, the imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Slow down, Professor, please, be so kind. Continue, please. I'm sorry for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The exception is an imminent threat of war or a state of war. We looked at those provisional decrees that only apply for as long as there is a state of war, and this is then adopted by the president of the republic for the duration. Under Article 90 paragraph 1 a decree is an act of the cabinet used to implement laws, other regulations and acts adopted by the People's Assembly in accordance with the constitution. Other articles discuss the manners in which this is done and how decrees and other acts are adopted in order to have laws implemented. Not in order to regulate any social relations such as a legislator would do by passing laws. There is a single case of what we call an autonomous decree. This is a decree adopted in order to autonomously regulate social relations. This is from Article 90, paragraph 5, establishing principles for the internal organisation of ministries and other bodies of state the administration. If you look at that particular decree in Serbia's Official Gazette and all the regulations are published there, you can see that it invokes the constitution Article 90, paragraph 5 or the implementation of which it was to be adopted to begin with. There are thousands of other decrees that were adopted, and all of them invoke the specific law for the implementation of which we were adopted to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It is precisely what the Professor has been addressing now that we find in slides 7 and 8. And in order to avoid repetition let us move on to a different subject matter altogether. Professor, I believe we have now sufficiently analysed Article 83 of the Constitution of Serbia. This is tab 5, P0855. Nevertheless, this entire chapter of the constitution entitled "President of the Republic," which includes Articles 83 through 89, all this is in relation to the president, right? Can we, please, briefly comment on Article 84 as the right of the president to impose suspensive veto. Let us clarify one thing first. This right is in relation to the power under Article 83, paragraph 3, where the president proclaims decree laws, whereas now here he has the right to impose suspensive veto. Can you explain that, please. ?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The right to suspensive veto is the right or the power of a president to send a certain law back to the People's Assembly for another vote. He can do this for two different reasons. Perhaps he considers the law to be incomplete, which is in the very nature of the institute of suspensive veto, or he can do this because he considers the law to be unconstitutional; although, this is not the meaning of the suspensive veto. It is not down to the president of the republic to judge the constitutionality of a certain law; this is something that the Constitutional Court should be in charge of. However, if you look at the provisions of Article 84, suspensive veto is not exactly a very strong or not exactly a primary power for the president of republic. The deadline is short as this creates a difficulty. The deadline is seven days -- as short as seven days from the time the Assembly adopts a certain law. This is all the time that a president has to study the laws and re-assure himself of the reasons that it is, indeed, necessary to send this back to the Assembly for another vote. The other reason is that this is no major lever in the hands of the president of the republic. If you have a vetoed law, the Assembly can simply pass the law again by voting by the same majority as previously, and then the president is duty-bound to promulgate this law. If a law is vetoed, it's not really discussed again. So this institute was not really a powerful tool in the hands of the president of the republic, except in such cases where in order to have a law that was originally vetoed passed, the majority that was required was the majority that was above the parliamentary majority such as that enjoyed by the cabinet. We see an example of this in the United States where what is required is a two-thirds majority in order to have a law that is vetoed passed again. In this case you need a same sort of majority as the first time around when the law was passed. This is no major power for the president you might say. I've been dealing with constitutional law for a long time, and I've never seen a country with a deadline this short for cases such as these, all of seven days to have a law sent back to the Assembly by the president for another round of voting. This is an exceptionally short deadline. If you look at this condition and you see that the deadline was then extended from seven days to a total of 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about this in 2.22 and 3.10 of your expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please bear with me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just been warned by my colleague that Article 84 -- the translation of Article 84, the very first sentence, it's a poor copy, and you can't really see the deadline by which the president -- the deadline for the president to send back a law to the Assembly for another round of voting, so that's seven days, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Seven days for the president to send it back to the Assembly and this is the same deadline for the president to promulgate a law, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, promulgate or send it back to the Assembly for another round of voting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, can we please comment on Article 85. You addressed this in 3.18 and 3.20. Could you please comment briefly on Article 85 of the law which concerns the power of the president to request the government to state its positions concerning certain issues falling within its jurisdiction, a brief comment, Professor, please, since we'll then be moving on to the relations between the president and other state bodies. You needn't look at your watch. I can assure you that this will not happen before tomorrow. Just a brief comment, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Under this article the president of the republic can request the government to state its positions regarding certain issues from its own jurisdiction. He cannot request for reports to be submitted to him by the government concerning the work of the government or the cabinet. The cabinet is not answerable to the president of the republic, but rather to the parliamentary majority, that's who they answer to. The president of the republic does not preside over meetings of the cabinet, this is done by the prime minister. The president of the republic is not the person who signs any enactments made by the cabinet; he cannot establish or abolish any of the ministries. He has no power to appoint the prime minister or any of the cabinets' ministers or to revoke them. This is all for the parliament and the relationship between the cabinet and the parliament is based on the principle of parliamentaryism; they answer to the majority for their work. However, the president of the republic can order to do what is his job. He can ask the cabinet to report back to him on issues from the cabinet's remit or jurisdiction. But nothing happens no matter what the cabinet says. The cabinet enjoys full freedom to state their positions in a forthright way. This is some sort of a report whereby the cabinet informs the president of the republic. This is something that is quite important in the president's work. This is not a vertical relationship between the president of the republic and the cabinet. This is coordination by state organs going about their state business.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will be discussing this tomorrow as well, so I'm not pressing the matter any further now. Can we please shed some light on Article 86 now, paragraph 5 specifically. This is the wording of the oath. What is the legal nature of the oath, Professor?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: If you look at Article 86, the oath is not a constitutional norm. The wording itself is not a norm. The wording is not included in the constitution since this is under quotation marks, and the same thing applies to all language in the world I think. Quotation marks mean what somebody else is saying. So these are the words spoken by the newly elected president of the republic whereupon he assumes his office as the president of the republic. The oath itself is not a legal norm, and it incurs no penalties. This is an act that draws certain legal consequences, and the same thing applies to constitutional law and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. I think we'll need to call this document up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have [Realtime transcript read in error "1D712"] 1D752, the German Basic Law Article 56, the oath of the German president. The law is from 1949 and it's been amended in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The tab number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have -- 44, I'm sorry, Your Honours. Tab 44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can all read that quickly. Professor, what would happen if the president did not take the oath or refused to take the oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He must take the oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but you say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- It's a prerequisite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You say it's not a constitutional norm, but what would happen if he didn't take the oath, he couldn't become the president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a hypothetical situation. You could ask the same question the other way around. It is the constitution that forces him to take the oath. I don't think a person could become the president without previously taking the oath, but that itself does not lend any legal force to the oath itself. In other words, there is no rule of conduct prescribed by the oath, no norms are prescribed. He takes an oath concerning certain values which are sometimes purely moral values, sometimes purely legal values, that he will comply with the constitution and the law. If you look at the German constitutional law, the president, while taking the oath, invokes God to help him work for the benefit of the German people, for the well-being of the German people that he will uphold and protect the constitution, and then he ends in saying: "So help me God." What if in his work he should not abide by these principles? What could that possibly mean? Will God punish him? Will he perhaps torture him in hell once he crosses over into the great beyond? So this shows what the moral value inherent in the oath itself really means. If we translate this into legal language, you can't base anyone's responsibility solely on the wording of an oath. A judge takes an oath, too. I was myself a judge of the Constitutional Court before I took up office with the Constitutional Court, I took an oath invoking similar values such as the oath we have before us right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have heard of your learned discourse, but I am quite intrigued by what you have said. Now, Judges have a code of conduct, and if they betray the oath they are subjected to penalty under the code of conduct because that's against the oath. The president also as a code of conduct, and he can be impeached if he betrays the oath. The question could be, as you said, that this oath has no legal value. Now, please kindly help me in understanding, can the president choose his own words for the oath? Can he fabricate his own words to the oath? It is correct that he may not be sincere to the oath, that's different, but then there are consequences for that and there are remedies for that, but can he choose other words? No, because the constitution has given certain words for the oath, and they are as good as the constitutional words. What I understand by your learned discourse is as if these words are redundant. Can legislature give redundant, useless, superfluous, meaningless words for an office as high as the president? I should feel grateful, sir, if you kindly would give us your own thoughts about so we better understand what is the meaning of the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, the president has to utter the text of the oath. He refers to some values that represent the spirit of the constitution, but not just the constitution, also the democratic order of a society. If the president is not guided by a loyalty to these values in his work, then he will lose both personal and political credibility. He will not be able to be sure that he would be elected again, because the people would see that he was not loyal to his oath, he did not abide by his oath. So this is more of a moral and political penalty rather than a legal one. But far be it from me to believe that an oath is a pointless matter. No. I believe it to be a very important dignified act. However, it is very difficult to base the responsibility of the president of the republic on the text of an oath. I apologise, I get carried away and then I speak fast. The text of an oath is not that of a legal norm. In an oath there is a lot of emotional and a lot of pathetic which cannot be found in a legal norm, legal norms are non-personal; whereas, the text of an oath usually has a lot of text that can be considered pathetic, that can be considered over-emotional. And we can see an example of that in Article 56 of the basic law of Germany which is a kind constitution of Germany and which was amended after Germany was united.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, when I was a much younger lawyer than I am now, the oath in a criminal court in Scotland ran in these words: "I swear by almighty God and as I shall answer to God at the great day of judgement that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth." It's loaded with emotive, religious, and some would say irrational content. But at the end of the day if I did not or the witness did not comply with it, he would be prosecuted and convicted of perjury, one of the most serious crimes we have. Now, are you saying that the oath of a president taking office doesn't bear that sort of definitive effect, it has no legal normative effect, is that what you're saying? So it must be different in some way from an oath that a witness takes in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The president of the republic can be held responsible for violating the constitution pursuant to Article 88. Violation of the constitution can only be seen as a violation of a legal norm in the constitution and an oath cannot be considered as such. The fact that it was put under quotation marks and the oath is the only text that is put under quotation marks further illustrates this. It is not my desire to diminish the importance of an oath. Somebody who is a candidate for the post of the president of the republic has to be necessarily a person of high moral values, and when such a person utters this text it has certain weight. And when -- but he will suffer moral consequences, not legal ones, if he fails to abide by this text. I cannot think of a situation where the Constitutional Court or whatever organ might judge the responsibility of the president of the republic who would find him to be responsible for not abiding by the text of the oath. As for perjury, yes, that is a crime. That is a crime all right. However, we do not have a crime of failing to abide by the text of an oath. In our criminal code a perjury is a crime for which a specific punishment is envisaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just one thing before I continue. I was put on alert that on page 106, line 12, there has been in the transcript instead of 1D712 should be 1D752 which is the oath of the -- Article 56 of the German Basic Law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, very briefly, please. All items mentioned in the oath territorial integrity, sovereignty, human and civil rights, preservation of the constitution and the laws, preservation of peace and so on, all these items are values on which a constitution is based, correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me give you an example of the oath taken nowadays by the president of the republic on the basis of the 2006 constitution. Among other things, he takes an oath promising to do his best to ensure that Kosovo and Metohija would remain within Serbia. This is beyond his control. What if the Security Council decides that Kosovo-Metohija would no longer be part of Serbia, would the president of Serbia be held responsible for violating the constitution in those circumstances where the president did nothing to diminish the territorial integrity of Serbia? No. This was a decision taken by the Security Council. You can look at the text of the oath which according to the constitution of 2006 the president has to take and you will see that there he takes it upon himself to do his best to ensure that Kosovo and Metohija would remain within Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: The mere fact that without the oath he cannot assume the office gives a legal shape to the requirement and that is law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would say that it rather gives dignity to the office, rather that than anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just one more thing and we are, however, close to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, sir, if we look at the oath in the German Basic Law which we can see on the screen, we see that the German president takes an oath to do justice to all. That is to say that everybody is equal before the law. However, it is not up to the president to ensure that everybody is equal before the law; rather, it is within the jurisdiction of the courts. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Based on this oath we can see that the president of the republic takes it upon himself to ensure peace and welfare of all citizens. So he swears that he will preserve peace and welfare of all citizens. Given that more than half of the citizens of Serbia do not currently live under good conditions, does it mean that all of those people can request that the president be recalled, stating that he violated his oath of office?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it is a proper place and the time is right to call it a day. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, that brings us to the end of our business for today. You will, as you know, require to return here tomorrow to continue your evidence, that will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Meanwhile, overnight it is essential that you have no communication with anyone at all about the evidence in the case, that's either the evidence you've given or the evidence you're going to give. Talk to anyone you like about whatever you like, but just don't talk to anyone about the evidence in this case. I hope you enjoy the evening. Please leave the court with the usher now, and we look forward to seeing you again at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Court is now adjourned.
